review_text: Very kind professor who will always be willing to work with you to help you succeed.

I love this man his lectures are a bit boring but he explains concepts so well and he is so enthusiastic and cute and awwwwwwwwww. Also he tells you exactly whats on the quizzes and exams and if you practice with the previous exams you will do well. pedram is the goat and i love this guy so much im taking him for 132.

Pedram Sadeghian, my goat. 

I enrolled in this class thinking it would simply satisfy a requirement. Silly me. What I actually signed up for was a spiritual awakening disguised as a computer science course.

Lectures? Cinematic. So good that my Physics friend understood data structures just by looking at this man’s beautiful smile. His voice? Soothing. He can put anyone to sleep in just 2 minutes. Somehow he takes topics that look like alphabet soup in the textbook and presents them like they’re the most obvious, natural things in the world. You leave class thinking that was so easy! Then you open his projects and past quizzes and realise that .

Sadeghian has this supernatural ability to make all his students feel like Batman. Because his quizzes and exams let his students unlock a new level of insomnia! At one point I’m pretty sure my laptop battery learned more from lectures than I did. I tested this by leaving my notes open next to the pipe that's leaking in La Plata, it’s now compiling code independently.   

If you are looking for an easy A? Run away. If you are looking for new ways to torture yourself that even guatemala hasnt invented yet

Also he's really hot and his shiny bald head WILL distract you during exams.

GENUINELY the best best best TA ever. Went above and beyond to explain concepts I didn't understand. She gave me confidence and made me feel so much better about the class.

Really bad, would not recommend you take her as your professor. Her lectures don't teach you anything at all, she will barley glance over topics and put them on the exam. 100% of the material will be self taught, and she often makes mistakes explaining things in class. The projects are not hard, however the exams require you to thoroughly learn the material on your own.

3.5 stars, genuinely she isn't as bad as people say. 

Honestly, I feel her reviews are a little too harsh. Her slides are pretty basic, but (most) the material is very similar to AP CSA, where there is a LOT of review material online on. I think Nora is incredibly nice, and her TAs were helpful in holding review sessions, but I do agree that she is not the best person to explain every concept in a way that sticks and is thorough. I think navigating Nora's 131 is knowing your resources and practicing, which seems like a lot but once you get a routine it truly isn't hard, I promise. I did the projects early on and diligently, watched YT videos for concepts that were difficult, used ChatGPT to generate quick intuitive notes to read and some practice questions. Note: CHATGPT IS NOT FOR PROJECTS, THAT WOULD ONLY BE CHEATING YOURSELF, lots of projects had high averages and the exams... not so much, please use those projects to your advantage and study productively so you aren't cramming and barely practicing. She did not curve the exams but they were pretty similar to the practice test/question bank she gave out. Exam 2 was a little more challenging in that sense but if you understood the lecture, wasn't too crazy in difficulty and you could piece the difficult questions together. The final had a couple challenging questions but nothing too wild. What to really emphasis in your study is PRACTICE, that's the only way to learn how to intuitively code in this course and beyond. Lastly, her lectures. Mixed feelings about this. Her lectures were really boring and I could almost swear half the class was doing something else. But if you needed to revisit, she had them recorded. I honestly felt, even though I didn't pay much attention, the general idea sank in and then I self studied later. Looking back, I wish I paid attention so I could save some time, haha, but self studying using the slides and online resources got the job done. That being said, I do have solidly decent prior Java experience so it wasn't all that foreign to me. If you have never coded before, this could be a steep learning curve, but in that case just power through the boring 50 minute lecture, genuinely try your best to understand+practice, and you should be alright, believe in yourself :) 

TLDR: If you end up with Nora, it's not the worst. Make a diligent self-study schedule, stick to it, and practice using her material. utilize all possible resources. you will achieve your goals. 

ALL THE BEST

Overall great guy and a chill professor. The class has a ton of work, but he provides so many resources to study. Make sure to review old topics for each exam so your coding stays up to date. he records lectures and is extremely nice.

Prof Aaron is a kind and funny guy. But if you come into this class with zero CS knowledge, you're cooked. What he goes over in lecture and teaches is NOTHING like his midterms. He gives past exams/practice exams, but again NOTHING like the midterms, so it's like you're wasting your time doing them. Whereas other professors make their midterms fair and based on the class material. He is also VERY slow with grading, and it's often impossible to know what you have in the class until the very end, and there's no way of predicting your grade cause he doesn't post all the assignments on Canvas. I highly recommend taking a different professor if you do not have background Java knowledge, because this class was insane. If you do end up having to take him, please go to office hours and do not fall behind. My TA helped me a lot, and I wouldn't have ended up with the grade I wanted without her. However, I am still giving him 3 stars because he was nice enough to round my 92.36 to a 93.

Teaching & Materials: He is a good professor in terms of giving the content clearly and having a lot of recordings, slides, and practice to look at during the lectures and discussions. However, he was a bit monotone so every lecture I attended kind of went in one ear and out the other.
Content Difficulty & Background: The content really was not that bad at all, but I didn’t take CSA in high school so I think seeing this for the first time might be the reason why a lot of people do poorly.
Exams: The exams throughout the semester were fair for me, but I thought the final was much more difficult than the exams we saw during the year.
Study Advice: Overall, I recommend reading through slides and watching through lectures to review. Practice exams/quizzes were way easier than the actual exams, so lowkey just focus on understanding the content, syntax, and definitions more than memorizing what’s on the practice exams because those concepts probably won’t be what’s on your actual exam.
Overall Experience: I am taking him for 132 too, so I had a pretty good experience!

Great professor. really chill guy and good at teaching. posts lecture recordings and slides as well as sample code to help. exams are hard and you have to handwrite code, but that's just what it is in cs. doesn't curve unless you are in between a letter grade then rounds up. 92.9 isn't a 93, but 89.6 is a 90. programming assignments are easy and a great grade booster (25% of grade). They also help with reviewing for exams and quizzes as the material tested with the code is what you're learning in class. Didn't go to office hours until final review, but he was helpful there too. Quizzes are announced and closed note. Labs are unannounced and open note, so go to discussion. Final was super easy compared to the midterms, was about 1.5 times the length of the exam but given double the time. Overall, if you can take him, take him. Easy to get at least an A-, even if you bomb exams. Kinda annoying he doesn't curve, but you shouldn't fail the class even without it, as long as you submit everything and show up to exams.

This course was significantly more difficult than other sections of the same course due to the instructor's exam design and grading policies. While rigor is expected, the level of difficulty combined with the lack of dropped assignments (even one quiz would have helped) created a grading structure that was inequitable across sections. 

Although this course was described as "beginner-friendly," in practice, it was not due to the nature of the harsh exams which did not reflect the difficulty of the practice he had provided. For students new to the subject, this made the course especially challenging to navigate.

As a result, receiving one poor exam score had a disproportionate impact on your final grade. This leaves no room for error for future assessments.

Students should carefully consider their coding background before enrolling in this section. Given the exam difficulty and grading structure, I would not recommend this course for beginners.

Pedram is a good CMSC131 Professor.

The lectures are really good at explaining the concepts. As a person who never took AP Comp Sci and wasn't familiar with OOP, he did a really good job explaining it and other concepts I wasn't familiar with like recursion. His drawings of memory maps really help you understand what's going on. The other reviews are right that his lectures can be a bit monotone and on days where I was a bit tired it was easy to drift off.

The projects are nice and straightforward and you shouldn't have trouble finishing them if you start on time and get help if you need it.

The quizzes and exams are all doable. I know some people say he has hard exams (and it does seem to be this way compared to Elias and Nora), but they're all doable if you know the content from the lecture and do the practice he gives you. He also gives you nice review material for each quiz and exam (except for the final).

Tips to succeed:
- Attend every lecture. Attending them in-person helps you learn all the content at a nice pace. 
- Attend discussion. Before quizzes and exams, they are very useful for review and letting you know what will be on the quiz/exam. They are also helpful for learning specific things you may need for the projects and giving extra examples/questions to solidify the concepts. Some content (not a lot) is only taught in discussion.
- Start projects early, try not to push them to the last minute. You’ll learn more from them.
- Have a plan to study for each quiz/exam. This doesn’t have to be super thought out, but plan enough that you don’t need to cram the day before/of. A decent bit of time before each quiz or exam, Pedram will post details about it on Piazza where he usually gives a worksheet to work through and past papers. At least, give yourself enough time to work through all of it without rushing. Do all the practice he gives you. Going through the code examples in the zip files provided with each slide and making sure you understand what’s going on can be helpful. Exams and quizzes combined are a large part of the class grade so prepare for them well.
One of the most understanding, knowledgeable, personable, and funny people I've ever met within the professional sphere of computer science. This dude is great, and buy his game on Steam.

She is a super nice person but not the best at lecturing or teaching the class. Her slides are really good and you can learn a lot from the slides. She shows the slides and does live coding demos in class. If you pay attention in class and have decent prior knowledge of the topics you will be ok. Honestly not the best prof but if you can learn on your own and read slides you will be definitely good for 131.
amazing professor! Very fair exams and rules

Pedram is a very good instructor: from what I saw and experienced, he always cares about his students and if you ever have any questions during lecture, he's more than willing to answer. Lectures were often broken up into 2 sections with a short break in the middle, and were always recorded with the slides being posted as well. I see a lot of people saying that he's monotone or lectures are boring, however I saw it more so as Pedram wanting to be as straightforward as possible when communicating content. Pedram and the TAs were also very responsive on Piazza for any questions that came up outside of class time.

CMSC 131 is just a tough course in general (in my eyes coming from someone who didn't have a lot of programming experience beforehand), however Pedram was always very approachable and helpful if there was something confusing and made it a bit easier. In my opinion, if you're willing to put in the work in classes, you will come away with a good grade, and learn a lot in the process.

Overall, Pedram is a solid professor. He explains concepts clearly ( even if boring) , is approachable, and makes the class manageable. He records his lectures, gives a short mid-lecture break, and provides detailed exam and quiz outlines, which were especially helpful when studying.
Where he tends to fall short is in exam alignment. The material taught in lecture and shown on practice exams is often much easier than what appears on the actual exams. As a result, the real exams feel significantly harder and less representative of what we are given. This is reflected in the exam averages, which were around a C surprisingly low for an introductory CS course where many students already have prior coding experience.
Because of this, I would not recommend this class with Pedram as a first exposure to coding. However, for students who already have programming experience and can handle higher-difficulty exam questions, he is a reasonable choice and overall a decent professor.

I think this is one of the most fair reviews you will get as this was my first ever computer science course ever. The only reason he is not a 1 star is because he records lectures, is a nice person, and does the bare minimum for previous quizzes and practice exams. But when it comes to being an actual professor he is simply not good at all. I do not get why other people are giving high reviews if they think he is boring. Many students skip his lectures because he often just goes through some half baked slides and goes on tangents about something we never need to learn or a concept we learned weeks ago in class. When it comes to teaching concepts, he does almost everything poorly except for memory maps which aren't on any of our classes exams or finals but it was for other students. Also his exams 1 and 3 as well as quizzes 3 and 5 were completely different and way more difficult then his practice exams. ANOTHER big issue with Pedram was his timing. We learned all the material for exam 3 way before thanksgiving break but instead our exam was right after break. Many people including myself would have much rather spent time with our families instead of studying for a class in which other professors gave their students their 3rd exam before break. All the other classes had way more time to study for finals and I was even using other classes study material to learn concepts because what Pedram gives simply is not good enough. Lastly, discussions were pretty much useless unless it was a day before a quiz or exam. I would learn a concept from brocode 10x quicker then a discussion, and I do not get why our quizzes were not in there like the other CS Classes so we could actually learn content in class.

Highkey a bum professor, his lectures are recorded but are very boring. This year he decided to change the curriculum, meaning that all his previous exams/quizzes were useless. This gave Pedram the chance to make them annoyingly hard, no matter how much you studied. If you know the material beforehand then you are fine, but if not then you might be in some trouble. This is known as one of the weed out classes, however no need for him to make his exams so much harder than what he did previous years.

The absolute best. Explains concepts very clearly and shows that she really cares about the students that she teaches during discussion.  If I could could give her 6 stars I would, you will not find a better TA than her!

Pedram is pretty chill, although I physically could not pay attention to this class because of how monotonous his voice gets. Lectures useless. His exams are hard compared to the other professors(comparing averages it was about 10 to 15 pts less).

1.5 stars. 

Pros: An okay lecturer and at least records lectures. 

Cons: 
1. Exams and quizzes are often completely different from practice exams and practice quizzes, as well as lecture material. Sometimes, topics which are said to be covered in quizzes and exams are not actually in said quizzes and exams. 

2. Does not review material in class in the days before exams. He does not provide any explanations for where points have been missed on quizzes or tests, or he just tells the TAs not to provide explanations.
 
3. Project descriptions are extremely vague, and expected input/output files for certain methods to be implemented are often written strangely and/or incorrectly; he does not provide expected inputs/outputs in project descriptions, and relies too heavily on student-written tests. 

4. The 12% deduction for submitting a project after 11:31 PM of the due date is way too much. Outright refuses to give any points if submitted after 11:31 PM of the following day. 

5. Literally 67% of project grades are dependent on code passing release tests, rather than on whether said code adheres to expected input/output or not. Even passing the public tests is a small percentage of a project's grade.

6. Never gives extended time accommodations for quizzes, tests or projects. 

7. Relies too much on Piazza and doesn't like emailing. 

8. Rarely available for office hours.

9. Has the attitude of a 6th grader and the maturity of a high school sophomore.

Take either Elias or Nora, twin.  Or at least use leetcode if you are taking ped.
didnt go to my discussion in 131 and she wasnt even my TA but I always watched her videos, clear and helpful.

Probably the only reason I ended up passing this class. Super helpful in office hours and in discussion. He explains concepts in ways that made sense to me even though I didn't have any prior knowledge.

Aaron is a great guy and I would say that he has definitely improved looking at his past reviews. I came in with little to no prior knowledge and just needed the class for a programming requirement (took CSP in 10th grade), and I still felt like I was understanding what was going on. I will say make sure you go to office hours, that was the most helpful thing for me. The main downfalls of Aaron would be somewhat slow grading, but that's a lot of professors at this school, and the exams. I don't personally think any of the exams were insanely hard, but it is just slightly annoying that he doesn't have any practice exams he created since he started recently. All in all, I would recommend Aaron. He makes class pretty chill plus you get like 3 2-day extensions on the programming projects.

Pretty chill guy, if you have a cs background the class is really easy. However, the practice exams he provides are testing on entirely different topics than the actual exams. Additionally, he hasn't provided much study material for the final, making studying a bit harder. If you aren't coming into the class with a cs background, expect to study a bit harder and to get creative with study materials. Otherwise the class is pretty free.
Tiffany is the best 131 TA!

no curves and makes exams & quizzes impossibly hard

for an introductory course in java, pedram puts you through misery and extended suffering

take elias or nora

Ali is a fantastic TA. He is super nice, really helpful with projects, labs and really helps you to learn the content. He will come up with metaphors that are literally unforgettable. He really does work hard to make sure you do well and really honestly cares about everyone. He even draws little doodles on your quizzes and really puts in the time. If your TA is Ali he will make your discussions more fun and really care about helping you to learn.

Probably closer to 3.5 stars. Lectures are kind of boring and hard to pay attention to because he’s kind of monotone, but he’s super organized. Always posts lecture videos and TAs post discussion videos. He tells you what kinds of questions and what methods you’re allowed to use on exam. Provides a lot of practice exams.

Pedram's lectures are a bit boring, he just goes over the slides, but he does go through everything and the material is pretty simple. In the course we had 5 quizzes and 3 midterms. The quizzes are pretty easy, but the tests are a bit harder. Every week he gives a project assignment which is not to difficult and should be free points for your grade. TA discussions are very helpful and they review before tests and quizzes. I would give Pedram a 3.5 stars.

Pedram is a great professor teaching a somewhat boring class that is CMSC131. I really love how this guy goes into crazy detail, and speaks about how stuff in 131 can relate to future classes. To be honest, if you already know how to code, you can get away with missing 80% of lecture, however you would be missing out on good bits of information about how java works, which I can guarantee not many know. I will say, the quizzes and exams are actually a bit challenging compared to what he teaches, DO NOT UNDERESTIMATE THIS CLASS. just cuz you got a 4 in CSA and knows the basics of OOP does not mean this is an easy A, this class still needs some attention (I learned this the hard way). Overall Pedram is the goat for teaching, but when it comes to exams and quizzes, they can be difficult, so keep this in mind when choosing him. I'm going to continue with him for CMSC132, so I do recommend bro.

Aaron is a good professor, and he is very adaptable to students who need extra time or have had circumstances in their lives. He doesn't really respond to emails, so I'd suggest asking him questions in person. Sometimes the exams are random. For example, we had our midterm 3 exam, and it was somewhat like the practice exam, but the amount of time given to complete that test was impossible. But he did give more time to the class, which was nice. Overall, if you come to this class without a computer science background, it's kind of cooked because he goes fast. I'd recommend going to office hours and discussion for guided learning and help on projects and etc. I came in with computer science knowledge, so it wasn't much of a hard class for me because I ended up re-learning concepts that I already knew.

In the beginning, there was nothing. Nothing but the calm whisper of despair, a dire foreshadowing to what would come next for the world. The world was in what we would call a juvenile state. Birds were quiet. Water, still. The familiar whistling of wind, silent. But the savior, Angelyn Pham, changed all of that with a simple wave of her hand. Just like that, life was brought to this world, and eventually evolved into the marvel we experience. Now? She's decided to extend her gratitude unto us CMSC students, such that we shall uphold her honor and show employers our glory.

Annie Nguyen, my lord and savior of CMSC131. 🥹 She saved my 131 grade from the dead and revived it to an A+. She's kinda like the final boss level of TAs. She doesn’t need to study the material; the material studies them. Every office hour feels less like class help and more like being front row at a TED Talk. THE GOAT!!!

Don't even get me started with her aura. When you walk into her office hours, Annie doesn’t respond to your questions; she reads your mind and answers it with the most well-thought-out, clear, and elegant response. She's built different. I always have a hard time paying attention because of how much awe I'm in when seeing her.

At this point, people should be taking notes on her. Professors should be citing her. Entire curricula should be rewritten in her honor. She's THAT good of a TA.

Best professor. Great at teaching and super understanding. TAs are helpful as well. Lots of practice exams and you will be well prepared for the exam as long as you go to office hours, discussion, and class. Lectures recorded.

She isn't aware of how poorly she conveys information and this translates into the tests feeling disjointed from where we are at in lectures. Our most recent test involved a coding question which required information we had just learned two days prior and was worth 40% of the entire test. The practice exams did not have coding questions of similar caliber.

The fact that I am paying tens of thousands of dollars to come to UMD, just to have this quality of teacher is totally abysmal. I don’t know if the CS department was in lala land or what while hiring this man. But this professor is an absolute joke. The CS department is better off hiring a homeless man from Baltimore to teach this class. The 5 stars are actual bots that probably already knew CS and are just rage baiting everyone with their reviews. 

My TA was a horribly smelling dude that showed up to discussion and quickly went through some code and left 30 minutes early. 

The inconsistency with professors at the UMD CS department makes no sense. Elias in contrast is just an easy A and makes CS understandable because he’s an actual teacher and not some dude off the street.

This class was a genuine disaster. None of the study material ever matched the content on the tests or quizzes. Yoon is a nice person I guess but you can hardly ever understand him and he really does not teach well. For people new to CMSC he tends to not explain many of the terms he is talking about. He quickly moves through units without any time for students to grasp concepts. You can get a B or A but it is genuinely very difficult and requires a LOT of time. If you get a bad grade in his class please do not think you are bad at CMSC, he's just a bad starter professor for CMSC.

I wish I could give negative stars. DROP HIM IF YOU CAN YOU WILL LITERALLY SPEND EVERY WEEK CRYING HE IS A TERRIBLE TEACHER. I thought I was just really dumb and almost reconsidered CS until I talked to other CS majors and realized he is known to be the worst. There are so many horror stories, the other teachers are not nearly as bad at all. SAVE YOURSELF AND DROP HIS CLASS

No professor has invoked such passion as Yoon has for me. I didn't come for the content. I came to see Yoon. Honest take on his 131 class now. He starts off teaching with a software called processing, which, especially for beginners, is really nice to help visualize programs, and write with higher level syntax. The issue - our first two out of three midterms were based on it, meaning we only started using legit Java halfway through the semester, which takes a bit of time to adjust to. It would have been more helpful to start on it earlier. 132 is supposed to be the stepping stone to this class, but it's a bit difficult when you only get a small bit of exposure to java. I didn't do bad in the course, but it could have been a lot worse. I'm not a perfect student, but I came to class every day, went to discussions. Many questions on the midterms were extremely extraneous, maybe a concept only discussed once, or even something that wasn't explicitly stated, that you were just supposed to stumble upon on your own. I studied out of fear that certain random, trivial concepts would appear. Maybe I even learned more than I would have with a different professor, just because of this. For some reason, I still enjoyed the class. Maybe ironically, but everyone is in the same boat, so you make what you can out of it. He is truly a professor who cares and will stay 30 minutes after class just to help you with any questions you have.

No class should require 25+ hours of studying for a single quiz, and yet that's what it took. This class actually burned me out and made me reconsider doing CS at all. Even my friends got sick of me tweaking out over his class all the time. Even with the extra credit, it was such a mess. Don't take it with him unless you want a therapy bill the length of one of his midterms.
Also all the five star reviews are very clearly just Yoon writing them himself.

The average final grade in his class is a 67% which is a failing grade or at least not able to progress to the next level of compsci. And I think that should tell you all you need to know about his quality of teaching and if you should take him or not.

Yoon is an interesting guy. His 131 class is definitely much harder than that of someone like Elias, so if someone else is available, do not take Yoon. With that being said, this class is not impossible. In the end, it is still 131, so the topics covered aren't that complex. What makes it hard is the exams and quizzes he gives, which end up having very low average. For this semester the exam averages were as follows, M1: 64, M2: 59, M3: 52, Final: 60. Obviously these are not great, but I think that they should have been higher. Exam 1 was definitely hard, but exam 2 was significantly easier, and had a lower mean. Exam 3 was hard, but the final was easier than normal. The projects and lab assignments are very easy grade booster, and account for a large percent of your grade. He also gave an opportunity for 2.5% extra credit that would be added on to your final grade percentage. I ended up getting a 91 with that extra credit, which curved to an A+. He does curve the class at the end, but I'm not sure by how much. Yoon is a nice guy, but the class is hard. Avoid him if possible, it's just extra stress you don't need.

TLDR: This class is hard, but it's very possible to get an A if you really understand the topics of the course and study the previous exams. Curves at the end of the course
switching to electrical engineering i dont want to do anything related to cs for awhile

I bet there's thousands of reviews that don't actually make it but if you're still considering taking Yoon even after the very many horrible reviews you deserve what's coming at you. He is a good guy always in a good mood like a nice huggable panda but omg I'd sooner slurp pasta off the floor at the Y than take his classes ever again. This was a truly a mentally draining semester with him. Take him at your own peril.

This was my first CS class ever. And it was also my last. I couldn't stay in it anymore (as someone taking it for the 4 "easy" credits). Maybe I'm just stupid, but coming in with no experience in CS, I found this class boring and exhausting. The jump in difficulty was extreme for me -- we went from coding animals using basic shapes to pong. I cried to my dad and dropped the class. I think Dr. Yoon is genuinely a nice guy. He cares about his students, but maybe he just also hates them at the same time. Otherwise, why would he make this intro class so stupidly hard? I did enjoy staring at his shiny, bald head during lecture, though.

Some of these bots are giving him a five-star rating for no valid reason, which is misleading to others. I hope that if it’s Yoon himself, he sees this and changes his teaching methods. I want to emphasize that I have no personal animosity toward Yoon; however, his teaching style has genuinely made me not go with computer engineering as a major. Please stop misleading people, whoever is behind that burnout account and being specfic like the one that was recently posted.

Keep in mind that 131 is a hard class no matter who you take it with, and some of these reviews are because people did not put in the effort. Yoon is an incredible teacher, sure his exams are hard, but they are not off topic. He really cares about his students and if you ask him a question or for advice he will go out of his way to help you. He is a very humorous person and this makes his lectures very enjoyable. When preparing for exams, make sure to go through all the relevant slides and examples because some of the questions he gives are either on there or very close to it. Sure, I had a hard time in this class, but I ended up learning and understanding more about the subject then I would with any other teacher. He does not deserve all of the hate that he gets, and I would 100% take him again now that I know what to expect.

Also he has a really awful policy called a "Good faith attempt" where if your coding assignment doesn't hit the requirements for it, then he will drop your grade a whole letter grade. So if you were to (somehow) do perfect on everything else in this class, except for one programming assignment where it barely hits the good faith attempt requirements, then instead of getting an A with a 95%, you have a B now.

To add to my last review of him, he also made a coding project that is due during finals week. Like yeah that's not the worst thing ever for a teacher but considering every other aspect about how bad he is the programming assignment is just the cherry on top for why you should avoid his class.

If you can avoid him please do, his lectures are an absolute snooze fest, he explains a concept on Wednesday then it's on the quiz on Friday. Not to mention he gives one practice quiz/exam and then it has little to do with the actual exam/quiz. I took this class at my previous university and I still could not understand what he was trying to teach even with the background knowledge that I had on Object oriented programming. The projects really aren't that bad as the instructions that he gives are really in depth on what he is expecting but the amount of projects he gives might make you go insane. I know that compsci classes give a lot of coding projects but I'm talking like he'll give a project, then 2 days into the project he'll give a lab coding assignment, and then 3-4 days before the first project is due he'll assign the next one. Please avoid him if you can.

Yoon is nice person, but should not be teaching this class especially. Projects are easy but exams are unfair and completely unrelated to any other work we do in the class. Most multiple choice questions are on random niche things that he talked about for 30 seconds and have one bullet point on a random lecture slide. He tests on things beyond the scope of 131, such as sorting algorithms. He also gets into convoluted explanations of topics that do not help with understanding the topic add hand. Avoid yoon if possible, especially for 131. If you have him be sure to go over all the lecture slides before exams/quizzes and do your own research on things that are not fully explained in the slides.
Great TA

Good professor. As the other reviews have said, he's straightforward, but monotone. I've found myself dozing off in his lectures a few times, but his lectures are good and easy to follow. You'll do fine if you don't start your projects on the last day and go to lectures.

Highly recommend him as your professor for 131, really ease you into college life or something.  

Projects: The projects are pretty easy, they shouldn't take you more than a couple hours. The only issue is sometimes Elias will be sporadic and assign one project that took sub one hour and then the next week assign one that is like 3 hours long. Also sometimes projects are due on like a Saturday or Sunday which is kinda meh, I prefer to have all my stuff done by Friday night but whatever. The projects are kinda fun though. 

Exams: The exams are quite reflective of the old midterms (and finals too) so it is worth studying pretty closely to the given old midterm reviewers. I would also just practice a few things extra like a memory map(blegh) or writing a class or something.  

Quizzes: The quizzes are fairly easy, open note and in discussion, Really just take a few notes with like 30 minutes of actually going over the material and you'll be good. Elias also drops the lowest quiz grade so it works out.

In my opinion, Herman is a vastly underrated professor. He has three midterms and a final, and each is worth about 15-18% of your grade. He posts a 20-30 page long practice test about a week before each exam, thats filled with practice questions that are formatted and cover similar content as the corresponding exam. Basically, if you do the whole practice test and understand everything within it, you are set for the actual exam. He also posts worksheets in the form of optional homework that are good practice for exams. In terms of exam grading, he and his TA's are generally pretty generous with the grading, and I often found myself getting a higher grade than I expected. In terms of lectures, he doesnt allow electronics, which didnt really affect me as I dont use electronics in any of my classes, but he tends to be a pretty good lecturer. He covers the material at a good pace, and is very open to questions about the content. Hes also pretty funny and seems to care about his students imo. He and his TAs have plenty of office hours, and when he didnt have time to cover certain material in class, he went out of his way to make videos about it rather than direct us to the textbook to learn it ourselves, he also gave everyone three pieces of candy for halloween. He does incentivise people to come to lecture and discussion by having "surprise" graded worksheets that are cumulatively worth about 10% of the grade, so if you go to lecture and discussion, you basically get a free 10% of your grade as the worksheets are graded on completion. He also has participation points that are worth 3% of your grade where you basically have to participate a few times over the sem, so another easy 3%. As for projects, none of them were super hard, I think the longest one took me like 3 hours, he released the grades for the first two fairly quickly but waited till the end of the sem for the rest of them. He gives long instructions for the projects which have a lot of helpful details and as long as you follow that and style your code correctly you should be fine, he also gave extra credit for some of them if you finish them before the deadline. Basically, Herman is a good lecturer who cares about his students and gives ample resources and grade boosters so you can get a good grade in the class, just make sure to attend lectures and discussions and you should do fine.

Larry Herman has a lot of quirks, and I can see why most people seem to dislike him; I, however, thought he was overall a good instructor. His lectures are well taught, and he explains concepts very well. Discussions are spent doing worksheets, which are occasionally graded for completion. He also will occasionally and randomly hand out graded worksheets during lectures--this, combined with the fact that he doesn't record lectures, means you should definitely attend as many classes as you can. His project descriptions are incredibly long and often repetitive, but this is also an advantage; you're essentially told exactly how to do each project in the description. I personally didn't find his exams to be challenging--anything he says in class or writes on the slides or handouts is fair game, and he will definitely test you on even things we spent the smallest amount of time on, but he gives a LOT of good exam prep, from the practice exams, the homeworks, and the discussion worksheets (he even admitted in lecture that he will sometimes pull exam questions from discussion worksheets, so definitely do the worksheets!). He has some negative quirks, such as not allowing electronics in class, having an interesting participation system, and being really touchy over being called a professor for some reason, but honestly the only strong negative I have for him is how incredibly long it took for everything to get graded. We had a total of 10 projects throughout this course, and by the time finals came around, we still only had the first three graded; it can be stressful, because you really don't know how well you're doing in the class if you can't know your grades until the very end.

Overall: Good lecturer & exams are very passable once you understand his format, but he has a bunch of odd quirks and he's an INCREDIBLY slow grader. He's not the best instructor out there, but definitely not as bad as some of the other reviews have said. If you're forced to take his class, don't fret! Put in the work and you'll do fine. I'm giving him 4 stars because I can't give him a 3.5.

I think people are too harsh on Herman; his average here is a 3.14, which isn't terrible, but the way I've heard older CS students speak about him is as if he is the teacher of doom and despair. (Note that I called him teacher DO NOT call him professor this will be the first thing he says on the first day and he may even spend 10 minutes giving a whole presentation on it later in the sem!)

The project descriptions are quite lengthy, but personally I would prefer this to vague descriptions where you have to figure it out yourself. There will be pretty much no questions left unanswered. Some projects are quite difficult, but honestly some of the ones I struggled with the most were also the ones I left until the last day or two, so I would recommend starting around three to four days before the due date. Also, make sure you read through the whole project description before starting, I know it's annoying but it's better than if you start to code and then realize you're violating project requirements, because sometimes you are prohibited from doing things that may be intuitive. Overall though, some projects were hard, some were easy, and also bombing one or two projects is really not detrimental to your grade. He also has some nice extra credit for a lot of them if you do it early and only submit once which is super nice.

As for exams, I genuinely think his exams were extremely fair. Herman gives super long practice exams that I usually found to be harder than the actual exam, if not about the same. To study I typically reviewed his slideshows, which he posts, and then did those practice exams and I did pretty well on all the exams. Even questions I got wrong on exams, I felt like they were fair questions to have been asked and things I should have known. One interesting policy to take note of, though, is the grading of multiple choice questions. These were usually the harder part of the exams. They are multi-select and you get 1 point off for selecting an incorrect answer and 2 points off for not selecting a correct answer. This is super important because if you are truly unsure, you should just select an answer because you lose less points if that's wrong than if you don't pick it and it's correct.

The lectures themselves can be pretty boring, but I do think they are super helpful. In hindsight, my worst project grade was definitely as a result of me zoning out in class when going over that topic. If you listen in class, you will be pretty set because he does explain concepts well and often uses people in the front row as examples, which helps get the point across. Also, he does like to make jokes sometimes during lectures and personally I really enjoy his humor. The lectures are not necessarily mandatory, but there are graded worksheets that pop up both during lectures and mostly during discussions which are about 10% of your grade, so you really should go. Also, those worksheets are super helpful to understand what exams are like.

As for homework, I'm ngl I did like 3 of them and there were probably around 10-12 not quite sure. The ones I did were helpful but they're all optional and really can just be used as additional studying.

Finally, just some interesting policies that Herman has. No phones, laptops, iPads, etc. If using technology is important to you definitely don't take Herman because he is very serious about it and will call you out every single time. Don't sit in the back row because he will tell you to move up. The damn pdf password really got me it's really annoying to have a locked pdf but also thats not really that deep. There is a participation grade for 3% and he is more likely to call on you if you sit in the front (not really that crazy but good to know). He doesn't do Canvas announcements but instead has a newsfeed that won't notify you when he posts and instead you have to remember to check (this really pissed me off but also not that deep, not sure why he does this). You also can't email him or message him because he won't answer, you have to go to office hours to ask any questions and such. Finally, he has very specific style requirements. Most of them were pretty intuitive to me, the only one that sucked was that you aren't allowed to have multiple return statements, that was always so annoying but I got used to it.

Overall though, I thought Herman was a very good teacher and I can honestly say I learned so much this semester. Coming from AP Comp Sci A in high school I think it's super important to have a good teacher in 132 for these foundational concepts. I know a lot of people where 132 was more review for them, but for me it was all new and I feel like I learned it very well. I recommend Herman for 132!

to start off, I want to clarify a couple of things:
1. this was the summer version, so 15 weeks of content condensed to 10 weeks

coming from someone who took yoon for CMSC131, pedram was a breath of fresh air. people say that pedram's voice is monotonous, but he legit sounds like a cartoon character and it makes listening to him so fun. try it, close your eyes and listen to his lectures and let your mind wander. 

overall thoughts:

something that really set him apart for me is how well he explains things. I never considered myself to be such a visual learner until I took this class. I appreciate that he takes the time to draw both the stack and the heap when explaining concepts such as recursion and the initialization of data structures. I found myself also drawing things out when I wanted to figure out the logic for my projects. he is really great at breaking things down and his slidesets are always very thorough and to the point. I also really liked that he included applications to the real world of what we are learning because it just makes what you're learning a lot cooler yk. 

projects:

the projects that he assigned were somewhat challenging but not to the point where they were impossible. i'd recommend that you just sit with a problem for a while because the answer will come to you eventually if you give yourself enough time. I'm not gonna lie, I lowkey enjoyed them. the projects are pretty much free 100s as long as you submit on time and pass all tests. the content from the projects will basically be most related to what he will test you on the exams, so it's important that you don't chatgpt your way through them.

quizzes:

idk if this is the case for fall & spring semesters, but our quizzes were not weighted very much and were open note save for the debug quiz (lowkey kinda a joke but appreciated). make sure you do well on them because they're a way to get some easy points. 

exams:

something that pedram does which is such a lifesaver is that he gives an outline of the exam two days prior to it. it contains the methods you will need to know for the exams, what the exam will and will not cover, and how many questions/what type of questions will be present. HYPERFOCUS ON THIS. you don't want to end up spending all your time studying something that won't even be covered. the previous year exams that he gives are good practice, but don't rely entirely on them. simply do the problems related to what the exams will test you on. the exams themselves were pretty fair. 

since this was a summer class, we had 1 hour and 20 min long exams for the first two exams and then 2 hours for the final. however, our exams were longer since we had more time. for the first time in a cs class ever, I was able to finish an exam in the allotted time for all 3 exams which was a win. I think maybe pedram has changed, but the exams seemed reasonable to complete in the time that he provided. I gotta say that I am not the fastest in terms of algorithmic thinking, but I still felt that I had enough time to complete the coding questions on time.

- start projects early, but you alr knew that (genuinely it's the best way to actually master concepts from lecture)
- also figure out the logic for your projects before your fingers touch the keyboard (will save you lots of strife)

Lectures/Discussion:

   - Discussions often teach new concepts that WILL BE TESTED, so it is a good idea to go. Also TAs' are very helpful
Projects:
   -  Projects often times are usually some sort of data structure clone with a couple of utility methods often attached with it [usually the best part].
   -  Projects are often good for understanding the inner working of certain data structures and are quite interesting in that aspect as well, especially the utility methods
   - However, projects (especially earlier imo) in my opinion  do a mediocre job of helping students understand how to apply said data structures. One could learn fundamentally how a structure works in a project, but when tasked to code an algorithm  in a scenario, may draw a blank.  Its like if you were taught how to build a car, then asked to drive it. One can infer but not without application practice [Some other professors do puzzle/game style projects instead]

Quiz: some challenging, some chill, but usually well timed. Do not slack off on them though, be mindful.

Exams:
    - Exams are generally formatted with a decent number of questions involving theory, and 3-4 coding questions
    - The coding questions particularly test algorithm development rather than coding methods of a ds (understandably and arguably more interesting as well)
    - Difficulty wise, the coding questions aren't exactly, "beyond our ability". They are decently designed questions which definitely push our algorithm skills to the limit. However the topic of exams became a big issue due to 2 main factors -> Time, Resources:
           - Time: Exams were wildly crunch in time, to the point that they are unfair. On average for a person learning these structures and concepts newly, it should take around 20 minutes per algorithm give or take a few minutes depending on question variety. However we have on average 3 of these questions on an exam + theory (although that part is not too bad) on a 50 minute exam. This often leads to serious time crunches and not enough time for someone to solve the problem with a correct solution. Hence why the final seemed a lot easier pacing wise since we actually had the time needed. This is most probably the reason for all the low test scores, and its not something to look over. Personally time was the biggest issue here.
          - Resources: Past exams given do not reflect the current difficulty. Yes this is intentional as you have probably seen in other reviews, but do not take that lightly. I am not here to complain about that specifically though. I believe  the main issue here is partly that but also the fact that we get very minimal practice on ALGORITHM DEVELOPMENT in this class. Our projects as mentioned above often task us with making methods of a DS, and only a couple Utils which is usually beyond the scope of our test (though those are decent). Aside from that there is no coursework that we have, no homework or anything of the sort to help us practice algorithm development. Highly reccomend students to do LeetCode or any other interview style questions for the data structures learned, as those are the kind of questions that will be on the test (difficulty may not match exactly but take all the practice you'll get). Arguably this will also greatly help refine fundamental skills for the future too. But in general there is a big lack of in class resources for this department.
    - Anyway do not take these lightly, they do require a lot of effort so be aware of that.


TLDR: I think Pedram's a decent professor with good TAs, but the time crunch on his exams primarily on the coding questions and lack of algorithm practice can make the class an unnecessary struggle. If you are someone who already religiously does LeetCode or any kind of algorithm practice outside of class/willing to put in that often insane amount of effort to finesse the exams quickly, by all means take him. But if you are new to all of these concepts and want to understand without the tests completely destroying your grade, maybe think twice.

Course: Despite the name, this is really more 25% Objected-Oriented Programming, 75% Data Structures and Algorithms. So don't go into this course thinking it'll be more of the same stuff as CMSC131. Any of the Java you learn in this course is really taught in order to understand the ideas and implementations of the Data Structures and Algorithms you use throughout the course. 

Lectures: I'd say it's very important to attend lecture. Pedram records so there's really no excuse to not go through it, especially since he does a really good job highlighting how the various Data Structures and Algorithms he covers works. He even goes over many of the algorithms that you'll need to implement in the projects step by step, so attending lectures will make the projects much easier.

Discussion/Lab: These were weird because they were more like a second lecture than an actual lab. These are generally miscellaneous Java topics that may or may not appear in a project/test. These are not as worth attending, with the only exception being when the TAs cover sorting algorithms. These are also recorded and you can also watch any TA's recording so if you didn't get a good TA for your section you can just watch the other TA's discussion.

Projects: Most of the projects in this course focus on implementing functionality of data structures/algorithms. Again, attending lecture helps a lot with these projects. Implementing the projects is fairly easy and shouldn't take more than a day or two. The main thing is to make sure you know how to debug your code and write student tests as secret tests are usually weighted around 10-20% of the grade. Main thing I'd recommend is writing student tests as you work on the project, I felt that helped me a lot with making sure my projects were good. Also try to maintain good style and write comments as you go so you don't have to deal with doing it all at the end. 

Quizzes: There are 5 quizzes of varying formats. 2 of them were "write code" quizzes. When Pedram asks you to write code he expects you to know how to write an algorithm that solves a problem from scratch. The main way you can practice this is through the practice tests and projects. He recommends you write the algorithm out on paper and then code it up on Eclipse. I'd recommend knowing how to trace out algorithms, pay attention to the specific details of the question, as well as practicing material that relates to what Pedram says the quiz will focus on. Another one was a "debugging" quiz where you sat with a TA and showed them that you can use the debugger. Just know how to use the debugger and it's a free 30 points. Last 2 quizzes are take-home "project" quizzes which simply involved you having to write a code piece on Eclipse, which are also free 30 points each since there are no secret tests with these quizzes and lecture + lab gets canceled that day so you can work on those quizzes.

Exams: Exams generally consist of 3 parts, Fill-In-The-Blank, Short-Answer, and Code Writing. For code writing my advice is the same as the code writing involved in the quizzes. For short-answer questions, I'd recommend knowing the slide material and knowing how to trace out any of the algorithms that you learn in class/implement in projects. Understand how the Java compiler works as that'll be important for understanding some of the concepts you need to know for these exams. For fill-in-the-blanks, again just review the slides thoroughly and use a tool like Quizlet to memorize key terms. 

Other Random Advice
- I didn't go to office hours (didn't really need to) but if you are struggling I'd recommend it. The TA's this semester were very good and helpful. If you have small questions, use Piazza, the TA's (and even Pedram at times) will respond quite quickly.
- Pay attention to Pedram's posts on Piazza, especially when he releases details about the Quizzes/Exams. He gives away a lot about what the test will focus on which will help you guide your studying. 
- Don't rely on the practice exams for your studying. While they offer some good material for practice they rarely if ever cover everything you'll need to go over for the test. Instead, try to create your own practice questions based on the slide material as well as study how you implemented the projects. If Pedram recommends you do a project before a test then make sure to do that project for practice. I'd also recommend practicing questions on the site Leetcode. Some of the questions are a bit advanced but the site offers good practice for questions related to certain data structures (especially LinkedList and Trees). 

Other Information 
- Exam averages in order were 66.96%, 67.05%, 78.31%. Final average was around 72%. Overall class average was 81.1% (this combines exams, quizzes, projects). Curve is unknown but I had a 96.28% and got an A+. 

Class Review: This was a great class and probably my favorite class this semester. Grew a real love for data structures and algorithms thanks to Pedram's teaching and the projects he gave. Exams are on the tougher side but are 100% doable if you pay attention to what Pedram posts about them and make sure to practice all the material instead of just relying on practice exams.

Was falsely accused by Kauffman last semester. Completely wrecked my relationship with UMD CS imo.

He published his own statistics on AI cheating in his class which showed that at least 19.6% of the class was penalized with a grade reduction or a pending XF case (XF is an academic integrity mark which removes CS students from the major.) Even more students than that were accused. 

On one project, he mass accused and penalized 15% of the class for cheating using compiler-generated code or AI because they used an "advanced" command, even though it was listed in the class slides, project rubric, project description, textbook, and an approved linked webpage on his course site. He also said we could reference compiler-generated code for the project and even bring AI-generated notes and content to exams, which makes it really unclear about what’s actually allowed. He originally accused even more students for the same issue until realizing he had accidentally included a non-project-related file in his checker. He said he had high confidence in the accusation, and offered a 0 to those accused on the project (~2% overall grade reduction) or a one-on-one interview process where success would lead to a regrade request and failure results in a XF recommendation to OSC. Over 1/3 of the accused students still showed up despite the existential threat of taking the interview, which makes me believe that he was really throwing around accusations. Either way, Kauffman later wrote in a post that he "was never once convinced of a student's innocence during an interview" and those who were let go only had "plausible deniability." The process was extremely stressful and lacked transparency.  

At the end of his course, 20 students in his section went to OSC. For context, there were 50 AI-related OSC across all departments and classes at UMD for the entire year of 2023, meaning his section last semester would account for around half of that. 

Whether you believe it or not, I know many people who were accused, didn't cheat, and were penalized anyway, including myself. His passive aggressive comments about not giving extra credit on later projects because of the cheating cases and verbal/written rants about "cheating" students devaluing the CS degree before any of the cases were even resolved made the class feel toxic, distrustful, and stressful like everyone was constantly under suspicion. On top of the difficult content, the threat of being accused and kicked out of the major over one or two lines of code on a project that is flagged as suspicious could seriously impact anyone’s mental health.

He may be allowing AI in future courses to avoid this issue again (or in his words, because too many people are "cheating"), but this is my two cents.

I'd like to start off by saying that he is not inherently the worst of the worst, I think that his approach at teaching is not the best, but I don't think he means it with ill-intent. I barely scraped by and ended with a 73% which resulted in a C, even after always scoring below the average on all his exams and quizzes. The way that the course was structured, at least when I took his class, was set up in a way that the projects and exercises made up a substantial part of the overall course grade. Lab works also made up a small but considerable percentage that can boost your grade by the time finals come around. If I am not mistaken at the beginning of the course, he acknowledged that his exams and quizzes were known to be difficult, but that as long as you completed the projects and exercises on time and tried your best in exams and quizzes you were going to be okay. 

Projects:
His projects were not inherently difficult, they were at times confusing, but attending office hours and posting on Piazza ultimately cleared any confusions you may have had. Exercises could often be done in a day, but I would suggest not doing this for both exercises and projects. Lab works were also easy to complete, and we were given enough time to complete them. Just by completing these on time, you can be at a good standing before exams and quizzes tank you grade (and they will, unless you are the type to ruin the curve.)

Exams/Quizzes:
His exams and quizzes were confusing, tedious, and soul draining. Often times it was never truly clear what exactly we were going to be tested on. Before exams or quizzes, he would send out emails containing a list of what we had covered since the previous quiz/exam, and he would say that what was on the slides was testable material, so it would be hard to differentiate what exactly was going to be on the test/quiz. On one occasion, what he stated was going to be covered on a quiz were assembly function calls and parent-child processes; given the difficulty and notoriety of his quizzes I studied everything assembly and assembly-function call related, and only studied parent-child processes some half hour before the quiz and ultimately the quiz only contained one assembly multiple choice question and the rest of the quiz was all related to parent-child processes; this time the quiz was easier than expected, but the angst and confusion leading up to the quiz takes a toll on you.

Part of the shortcomings related to quizzes and exams *could* be attributed to a student's lack of complete familiarity and understanding of the material, however, unless the only thing you have going for you is school (and that is okay, great actually, if it's the case for you - it is not often, rarely actually, for that to be the case for everyone) then it is very difficult to develop mastery of the material in time before exams and quizzes. Some topics may be covered a lecture or two before an exam/quiz and some of the questions on quizzes and exams feel like they are meant to be 'gotchas' or may be super specific to a covered topic. For example, though the understanding of unix commands is useful in various industries, some questions often relied on a lab discussion slide that may have shown some [blank] unix command that was only used then and never really again - to some students those questions may have felt like free points, but when you are handling other courses and only have a vague idea of what was to be on a quiz then, some miscellaneous unix command would feel like the least of your concerns.

I personally scored poorly on exams and quizzes, at some point getting a 39% on an exam, fully tanking my grade and putting my chances to pass on the line. However, because I submitted all other projects, exercises and labs on time, my grade was brought up just enough to pass.

Yoon as a person:
Results may vary, but Yoon was extremely approachable and a kind understanding person. If you come to his office hours or email him, he is very helpful and he often responds to emails fast.  I often stayed after class to ask clarifications or questions related to the content, so did others, and he would make sure to explain and breakdown your confusions so as to help you better understand the material. Moreover, if you maintain a clear communication with him about certain issues and difficulties, he is often willing to help and possibly grant small extensions for submissions. He is also kind of funny when you talk to him one on one. I would say, do not walk into his class seeing him as some sort of evil supervillain who sits in his office petting a cat while plotting on how to make his next exam as hard as possible. If I am not mistaken, being a professor is not his main role at the university, take a look at his extensive resume and his achievements and you sort of realize that being a professor is just a role he has to play, and he can only have so much time on his hands, so balancing all of these responsibilities may be difficult even for him. 

p.s. I say all this not to glaze him or hype him up, all I'm saying is that it's probably a lot of work to handle but he's kinda goated if you talk to him - ppl like to make him seem like the devil himself but he's not too bad.

Yoon as a professor:
Now, regarding his teaching style, it is not really the best. Attend all his lectures and you will realize that not many people show up. He likes to go into a lot of specific niche topics while teaching, and he likes to draw on his iPad to breakdown what may be happening regarding memory allocation and a lot of other visual stuff. Often times this gets confusing, as he draws on top of the slides, so it is not visually the best and easiest thing to understand unless you follow along closely. If you walk into class during these moments when he draws out topics, it looks like that one picture 'my coworker losing his damn mind.' Moreover, sometimes he goes back and forth with a lot of coding examples and slides, so it gets a little confusing to understand. It is hard to keep up sometimes and it would often require revisiting his recorded lectures to get a better grasp of a concept. On the times he does do well, then it is easy to follow along and he does a good job at walking you through some of the topics. 

Class logistics:
Honestly not the best at all. This semester, we only found out about our exam results a couple of days before the final. Some projects take a long time to get graded, and the late submission turns on after 11 pm of the on-time submission date. Some lab works were graded the day of grade submissions, so it was difficult to truly get what your grade was throughout the semester. Honestly, it was gut wrenching not knowing where you stood before the final exam was added to the grade book. He would often curve, at some point in some semester he curved by 8% percent, but this semester he did not curve as much, only slightly so that was also gut wrenching. 

TLDR: Not the worst. His exams and quizzes are hard and may tank your grade, but the class is set up in a way where your grade is able to take it if you do all the other work on time. As a person he's chill, as a professor he struggles, your grade will never be truly clear until the day grades are due. If you have to take him because every other section is closed prepare for a rough semester but if you show up and do your best you should be good. Not truly the end of the world, but you will have to put your head down to make it through.

To whom it may concern,
Yoon's exams can be challenging. To do well on them, make sure you really play around with edge cases on the compiler, modify the lecture example code. Do not think about this class as a class about C, just how bits and such are set. Assembly will inevitably feel hard, just practice and it should be ok. For projects, many of the hidden test cases are decently predictable, make sure your program can handle what the spec says it should handle. For example, if you are making a playlist program and the spec says the number of songs will never exceed 80, make sure you test how the program handles an empty playlist or a completely full one. They can really take a chunk out of your grade, but these hidden tests are usually just testing small edge cases. Make sure you check gradescope for the lab assignments as they aren't always announced. He sets cuttoffs at the end, I think they were lowered by around 3% for my specific scenario. He is a really nice guy.

Kauffman is an amazing CS professor. I would 100% recommend taking him. That being said, here is how his class works:

Lectures are 75-minutes, he records everything, but it is still helpful to attend since he is a good lecturer and he takes a lot of questions during lecture. Each time you ask a question, it counts as extra credit. 

Discussions are pretty much free. We are required to complete at least 10 labs for the course (there are 12 labs in total).  The TA will pretty much give the answers to the lab in discussion and you're allowed to collaborate with others on it. On top of that, close to project deadlines, discussions are converted to extra office hours which can be pretty helpful. 

It is really easy to get a 100% on every homework since it gives you the option to submit each question and the entire form. After every question, it tells you whether or not your answer was right, and you can keep resubmitting until you get all questions right. 

The projects are very long and difficult. Start early cause office hours (located on the 4th floor of A.V. Williams for some reason) fills up very fast and it can be either very hard or not possible to get help around the project deadline. In terms of difficulty, I found projects 1, 3, and 5 to be the most time consuming. Project 3 was both the most difficult and time consuming since it was the assembly project. The late penalty is very lenient, so there not much of problem with turning them in late. 

The exams are open note, but they can be quite hard. Rather than focusing on memorizing random things, they try to test big picture concepts and your ability to understand and apply them to sample programs given. There is no multiple choice, only short answer and coding questions. Furthermore, the exams can be a time crunch since almost all questions need a detailed response, so it's very easy to run out of time if you don't manage it on the exam. 

Despite how hard the projects and exams can be I still recommend taking Kauffman since he is a great teacher, a really nice and helpful person, and you will learn a lot of useful concepts from his class.

Good lecturer, fair exams (if you study and considering that they're open note), and extra credit on projects/exams/lectures. 216 is a hard class at Maryland but Kauffman is probably your best shot for learning. Take Nelson if you want an easy but less in depth class.

Fawzi is my favorite professor I’ve ever had so far at UMD, at least as it stands through my first year. I’m going to preface this review: I took MATH310, another proofs class in the math department, a semester before this class, and as a result, knew almost all the proofs content (about 2/3 of the course) beforehand except for modular arithmetic. I still went to his lectures though. Full breakdown below:

Lectures:
Fawzi is probably the best lecturer I’ve had at Maryland. I had a subpar professor for MATH310, and as a result, struggled with proofs worse than I had struggled with any math class in my life (as someone who considered myself a math person). I managed to salvage a 78% in the class, but I was for sure no expert in proofs before taking this class. Fawzi has a way of breaking down concepts in a very simple, easy to follow, and entertaining way that makes his lectures really easy to follow and understand. I feel like as a result of taking 250, I understand proofs way better than after MATH310.

Exams:
He did complain that he wrote exams that were consistently too easy and mentioned they were going to get harder, but they never got harder, so I’ll take it. His exams consistently have pretty high scores, take mostly lighter content from the lecture, and are basically what you expect from going to lecture. He can be somewhat nitpicky on proof structure, but there’s no math professor out there that DOESN’T nitpick proof structure. One thing I will say is he can sometimes grade things pretty harshly with regards to partial credit.

Quizzes:
The pop quizzes are the biggest issue with this class for me. They’re mainly a way of keeping people going to discussions, since any given discussion can have a quiz, so you have to go to all of them. All the quizzes are pretty straightforward, and you should normally score 20/20 on them if you’re keeping up with the material. Don’t be afraid to send a regrade request if your grade is messed up and you have an equivalent answer, but don’t send any begging for partial credit (the same applies to exams). He won’t budge on that.

TL;DR: Fantastic lecturer, pretty simple exams, and nice person. Not a fan of pop quizzes in discussion go. I feel like if he recorded lecture and announced quizzes, he’d be rated much higher, but he is 100% worth taking for any CS class.

I think Fawzi is a pretty reasonable professor. Firstly, he's (generally) a great lecturer which I appreciate more than I can convey considering I am someone who usually goes to her classes. Secondly, his exams and quizzes are pretty straightforward if you attend his lectures, do the discussion worksheets, complete the homeworks without cheating and actually understand them, and practice a bit on your own. I got an A+ in this class and I (almost certainly) promise you can too. Here's how:

1) GO TO LECTURE. Do it. Fawzi will tell you things in lecture that you will not get off the slides. Exam #2, he told us to review definitions. What do you know? We're asked to write out a theorem on the exam. The people who weren't in lecture were cooked. You probably will be too because Fawzi clearly puts a lot of emphasis on going to lecture.
2) Pay attention in lecture. I try to take notes while he's talking but do whatever works for you. This will make step #3 significantly easier.
3) If he does a problem in lecture, do it again, by yourself, at home. This is a 4 credit (I think) college-level math course. You're not going to learn everything just by sitting in lecture. If anything isn't absolutely crystal clear to you (and even if you think it is), do it again. This really isn't half as hard as it sounds as long as you do it immediately after lecture instead of allowing the lectures to pile up. I would take notes in pencil on paper during lecture and rewrite them on my iPad once I got home, based on his lecture slides.
4) If he gives you a worksheet in discussion, do it and understand it. A lot of times, our discussion quizzes were practically lifted from the previous discussion's worksheet.
5) Do your homework and understand it. Usually the level of difficulty of the homework is harder than the exams but every once in a while, we'd get a homework question on the exams.

Do all of those things and you'll be fine. The only reason Fawzi gets one star off is because on the final exam, there was a bunch of weird stuff about ordinals and cardinals and equivalence classes that I didn't feel adequately prepared for by the class. Honestly, I'm just being petty and his real score is more like a 4.5. 

Anyway, I really enjoyed this course and would happily take it again.
