nelson markets the class as "the easiest a you'll ever get in cs", and he isn't wrong per se. the projects are fairly straightforward (and the majority of the code for them can be found scattered across his lecture examples), although i know some students had issues with mongodb, which was in the last project so i'd definitely at least set up your projects early to troubleshoot potential issues. the exams for fall 2024 were also very similar to spring 2024, although spring 2024 was completely different from fall 2023, so take that how you will. honestly, this class is pretty chill if you're just looking for an upper level cs course, but is also very basic in what it covers (html, css, js, node, express, mongodb). nelson himself is the goat however so 5 stars

I don't really understand all the hype around Nelson; he comes across as a condescending teacher. For 335, the first midterm felt like a chore, requiring you to memorize a bunch of random information. The only effective way to prepare was by studying previous midterms. For fall 2024, our midterms were nearly identical to those from the previous spring, but they’re always subject to change—spring 2024's midterm, for example, wasn’t like fall 2023's. Our semester got lucky with similar midterms, but overall, you don’t learn much in this class.

I was in the 8 AM section, and while I didn’t mind the early timing, Nelson's lectures were quite boring. He often makes jokes and gets off-topic, which isn’t what I want to deal with at 8 AM. It feels like he doesn’t fully understand the material he's teaching. When asked for specifics, he often can’t provide clear answers. If something in his code doesn’t work, he doesn’t seem to know why.

I already knew the basics of HTML and CSS but wanted to learn more about JavaScript and MongoDB. Unfortunately, I was disappointed—Nelson simply gave us the code for those topics without explaining how the systems work. The final exam was super easy and almost identical to Project 5. You could literally reword that project and still get full points on the final.

The TAs are often PhD or master’s students, and they’re difficult to work with. They don’t provide helpful answers most of the time. This class is definitely worth taking if you’re in it for the grade, but it has its downsides. For example, the midterms aren’t given during class; instead, they’re held at 6:30 PM in a different lecture hall. While I understand Nelson’s intent to prevent one section from sharing answers with another, this setup is inconvenient. I would much prefer taking the midterms during class.

Overall, I think 335 needs to be restructured. It feels outdated and poorly designed. We had to learn things from JavaScript ES5, which is deprecated—why bother teaching it? I wish they’d reduce the focus on CSS and introduce more relevant topics, like React, into the projects. A more modern framework would make this course much more worthwhile.

As I am writing this, Justin's average rating on Planet Terp is a 4.69, which is even higher than Christopher Kauffman's average rating (4.63). I had Kauffman for CMSC216 in Spring 2025, and he was one of my favorite professors of all time. Needless to say, given all the hype around Justin, I had high hopes going into his Summer 2025 CMSC351 class. Now that everything's over, I can say in short that I am disappointed with my experience.

To be clear, Algorithms as a Computer Science class is commonly agreed to be a terrible class pretty much everywhere (based on talking to many people from many different universities). A large part of this is due to the fact that those with minimal experience in algorithmic programming find the class extremely difficult, while at the same time those with a lot of experience in algorithmic programming (i.e. competitive programmers, like myself) often dislike how it is taught very mathematically rigorously yet with little intuition or application at all (in other words, this class will not get you through a coding interview). Yes, Algorithms, the Computer Science class, is more of a math class than anything else. Yes, Computer Science is not just programming, and Theoretical Computer Science consists almost entirely of pure math. All of this I knew going in.

None of this prepared me for when I lost over half the points on a problem from Homework 1 asking me to prove the Big Omega of a certain function. I approached it as almost everyone intuitively would; like almost everyone had been taught to solve an inequality since middle and high school. Set up the inequality. Turn it into an equality, and solve the equality. Determine which side of the solution to the equality contains the solutions to the inequality, and turn the solution to the equality back into an inequality. Apparently, this wasn't rigorous enough for this class. Perhaps this is just how this kind of stuff works. But we were never told that solving it this way would lose us points, and the "correct" way shown in lecture seemed unnecessary and unintuitive. Instead, Justin complained that many submitted solutions to such Big-Omega or Big-O proof problems looked the way AI would solve them, and that such proofs "were generally terrible", citing several reasons why. Okay, fine.

If you take Justin, make sure you explain the hell out of any answer you give to a problem. One problem on Exam 1 asked me to find a lower bound for something and to show my work. I later received minimal points for my answer, despite the fact that the work I had shown lined up almost exactly with a potential full-score answer as described in the rubric. Upon submitting a regrade request, I was told the grader had no idea what I did here at all, since I had no explanation at all. But the question never asked me to explain! Too bad.

There was an Exam 1 MCQ problem which asked whether a certain algorithm was O(N^2) in the best case. The algorithm in question was O(N) in the best case and O(N^2) in the worst case. As such, most people in the class answered incorrectly, as technically an algorithm which is O(N) is also O(N^2). A big stink was made on Piazza about this being a trick question hidden in a sea of 50 multiple-choice questions, designed to make students lose points even if they understood the concepts it was supposed to be testing. One student asked, to avoid confusion, why didn't Justin instead ask if the algorithm was O(N^100) in the best case? Another student literally included a screenshot of the Merriam-Webster entry for "trick question" in their post. In the end, Justin's response was that technically the algorithm was indeed O(N^2) in the best case, and that he didn't expect his students to autopilot any questions in his class.

On top of this, there was a question on the Exam 2 MCQ which, depending on your interpretation of the question (the wording was not specific enough), could have had two different answers. However, if you picked the wrong one, you had no recourse, not even through Piazza. By this point, people had long since stopped posting on Piazza about questions like this. They knew nothing would result from their efforts.

On Exam 3, there was a free-response question which essentially asked us to find the shortest path between two points in "a simple, connected graph" (I'm simplifying greatly). Many test takers realized quickly the looseness of this wording and realized that, to cover all graphs which could potentially be described as "a simple connected graph", one needed to run Floyd's Algorithm, as a simple BFS would not cover the case of a weighted graph, and Dijkstra's would not cover the case of negative-weight edges. Once Exam 3 was graded, everyone who wrote such a solution to that problem lost points (there was a special "tier" in the Gradescope "rubric" for Floyd/Dijkstra solutions). I asked in my regrade request what the issue with my answer was. The response was that I needed to specify what my input to Floyd's Algorithm was or what graph I was going to run it on. I responded that in my answer I had specified running Floyd's algorithm on precisely the graph described in the problem statement. The response? "It does not define distances". Confused and a little frustrated, I wandered over to take a look at the official Exam 3 solutions. The official solution to that problem? Run a BFS.

Justin is not the worst professor I've ever had (currently, that (dis)honor goes to Manoussos Grillakis). Justin is not the devil. Justin is not someone who you need to avoid at all costs. But as a student in his Summer 2025 CMSC351 class, I felt like the environment I was in was just a little bit more hostile than I was used to. Every time I made a Piazza post, I was just a little bit nervous that I'd get flamed by Justin in his response. But for more security in your grade, I’d suggest the following approach:

Attend Ting's first 2–3 lectures to gauge how well you can follow along. Then, consider attending Justin's lectures (I started around the Big-O/Big-Omega/Big-Theta topics) and see how you find them. Personally, I found Justin's co-teaching more helpful for understanding the material, even though it meant waking up at 8 AM. By the middle of the semester, I stopped attending Justin's lectures in person, instead reviewing his notes when doing the homework. I also used office hours to clarify concepts and help others out, which helped me practice the material. Occasionally, I’d attend Justin’s 8 AMs just to refresh my understanding. Grade Breakdown:
MCQs: 7.69%
Homework: 15.38%
Exams: 46.15%
Final Exam: 30.78%
Total: 100%

Most of the MCQs were straightforward, with about 14 in total this semester. You should be able to score 100% on most of them, though the number of MCQs and homework assignments may change each semester, as well as the number that are dropped. Many students, including myself, used a group chat to compare answers, and we attended office hours for clarification on more open-ended questions. As for Ting's exams, there’s a good amount of partial credit, so even if you make a few mistakes, it’s rare that you’d need to request a regrade. However, exams accounted for roughly 77% of our grade, so even if you perform well on homework and MCQs, you still need to do well on the midterms and final to get an A. Trying to accurately reflect on CMSC351 with Max is a challenging endeavor.  It'd be far too easy to say something like "Max not Justin despite coteaching, therefore bad."  I don't think it's that simple, especially since I already don't have the highest opinion of Justin for CMSC351.

First things first, lectures.  Currently, Max just doesn't pull off taking notes live during lecture like Justin does.  He often spends a lot of time during lecture just on taking notes, presumably from his own reference.  This takes away time he could be using to properly work through examples, since he is fairly unclear and/or makes mistakes on some of the examples in lecture.  I don't think Max is experienced enough with the material to pull off live note-taking without sacrificing something else about the lecture.  I think lectures would be much better if he mainly used slides for introducing material, and worked out examples live to emphasize the major takeaways.  Max certainly has the energy to be a good lecturer, but the lectures this semester weren't great.  It doesn't help Max's case that he was out for many lectures where one of the head TAs, Lana, took over, and honestly I thought she was a much better lecturer.

Next, the inconsistency with Justin.  I could whine about exams here, but I'll save that for a bit.  My main issue with inconsistency actually comes with the different notions Justin and Max used for a few of the algorithms.  Two notably come to mind: Dijkstra's and Floyd's.  In a cotaught class, even if the exams are different, I believe that the content taught across the two sections should be the same at the very least.  With Dijkstra's, Justin's notes, lectures, and psuedocode were very clear about how the algorithm should be interpreted in the context of the class, which is done to get everyone on the same page when doing Dijkstra's algorithm problems on homework and exams.  Max's students needed to know Justin's interpretation because we had Justin's homework throughout the course.  It was very clear that Justin's interpretation of the algorithm records the shortest path between the start node and every other node reachable in the graph, whereas Max's interpretation has the algorithm stop upon reaching a destination node.  I actually brought this up, which Max agreed with me, and both interpretations were made acceptable for that problem on exam 3.  Something in the same vein happened with Floyd's algorithm, where Justin's interpretation had a "Pass By" for each node in the graph, where Max's was something completely different.  This wasn't the worst thing in the world, because the Floyd's algorithm problem on Max's final was explicit in exactly what it wanted (shortest paths of every node to every node where the maximum number of edges on each path is 2).  However, the sentiment is the same.  Something related to this point is that Max's section did not cover shortest path algorithm, but covered bucket sort where Justin didn't... for some reason...

Alright, now it's time for exams.  Simply put, these exams were very experimental, and they did not work with Justin's grade weights of 1/6 homework, 1/6 per semester exam, and 1/3 final.  The first exam was structured very similarly to a Justin exam, except with a Leetcode easy at the end.  Oddly enough, this was the only exam I got an A on, despite the fact that I'm typically horrendous at Leetcode.  Regardless, people were vocal about despising it, so Max changed the exam structure entirely for the following exams.  Each of the following exams had a few Justin-style "run through the algorithm" questions, but were majorly based on more theoretical questions which I turned out to be terrible at.  Exam 2 had 30% of its score determined by 6 multiple choice questions, and some of the questions were poorly written and/or relied on knowing niche facts before you could even come close to a valid response.  Exam 3 was mostly fine, but two questions in particular emphasized memory, which isn't something we really practiced in class in any capacity.  The final was mostly fine, but a few of the questions were weighted a crazy amount, and there were a fair amount of gotchas with small, but significant point reductions throughout the exam.  I did not clutch up on the final, and I screwed up so much compared to how I wanted to do that I only qualified for an A- with a small unknown curve.  I'll take it, but at the same time I wanted to do better in this course, but I didn't know how to prepare for the exams.  I'll accept that this is a pretty big skill issue, since the exam distributions throughout the semester were honestly pretty high for both professors (Justin's were typically a few points higher on the mean, with exam 3 having an 8 percent mean disparity, but Max's averages weren't bad).  However, I also don't think this class structure was setting most people up for success, and it didn't seem that we were given much leeway while Max was figuring out what he wanted his exams to be like.  It's honestly a shame, because I can see what Max was going for with the exams.  But they simply don't work with the grade weights we were given, and after exam 1, they were mostly independent from Justin's homework which we had to do throughout the semester.

I'm conflicted.  I want to give Max a higher rating, because I genuinely believe that this class wasn't designed to hurt the students.  Max may have some amount of arrogance or whatever, but he is genuinely willing to hear you out on issues you may have, especially if you have valid points when it comes to regrades (personal experience).  However, what keeps my rating low is that this run of CMSC351 was just rough.  I feel like a lot of decisions were made just to be made, rather than for the benefit of the students.  In a sense, it was almost like taking two different algorithms classes in the same semester.  For homeworks, we had to be good at Justin-style questions, which tended to be very specific in what they were asking and the answers they wanted.  For exams, we had to be good at Max-style questions, which tended to be far more vague and/or theoretical, but the answers they expected were still very specific.  It was very tiring.

Before I get into my review, I should note that the C+ is pretty much entirely on me. I should have taken the course more seriously, especially for the first midterm, and I got burned for not doing so. At least I passed.

With that said, this class did not work for me whatsoever. It's not because the class is hard, though it absolutely is, and I'd argue it should be. I just don't think it's for the right reasons. For instance, the lecture/exam half of the course is almost entirely disjoint from the GeekOS project half of the course, and it really feels like a 5/6 credit course sometimes. Being good at the lecture content will not help you whatsoever with GeekOS, and vice versa. This seems to be a 412-wide issue.

Regarding the lecture content, I don't think Pete is a very good lecturer. It's sort of what the other reviewers this semester so far have pointed out. I wouldn't quite agree with the tin can rattling mentality, but he certainly doesn't practice his presentations, and he brings absolutely no energy to the class. Another reviewer pointed out the ChatGPT image, which he said he would fix and never did, but there was another instance where he took a TRIO slide set from the internet, didn't review it at all beforehand, and tried going through it in a rather miserable showing. There's very little transformation of his slide content in his lectures, as all he does is take his laser pointer and point to things he wants to emphasize on one of the projectors in the room. The slides themselves are rather poor summaries of OSTEP, which he follows very closely.

That's just lectures themselves. The assignments he gives aren't much better in my opinion. He assigns weekly Gradescope reading homeworks which are worth 1% of the grade each. I honestly almost wish he would give more traditional homeworks instead. Some of the questions are horribly ambiguous, there's no room to state any assumptions, there are some questions where it feels like even with both the slides and OSTEP you can't really answer well, they ultimately lack engagement, and they are nowhere near comprehensive enough to actually prepare for the exams imo. Regarding exams, exam 1 was insane with the short answer questions of random topics from the slides being worth so much of the grade, while exams 2 and 3, especially 3, were relatively more chill. These certainly weren't my strongsuit, as I'm horrible with memorizing topics which I haven't worked directly with in some meaningful way, and I'm rather terrible at studying. I didn't like them, but they were fine I guess. One question I would like to address is the barber shop semaphore problem in exam 2. Not only were the semantics poorly defined, as the professor admitted, but in my experience, semaphore programming isn't just something just I get right away. I haven't worked with them before, as I haven't had any need to. They really weren't gone over well in class, nor were the gradescope assignments enough to really nail it in. He didn't give any other practice problem on them besides the baboon problem from a reading homework. I realize this is just one specific example, but it's emblematic of my problem with this part of the class as a whole. I also realize this could just be me, and my review should be taken with at least a grain of salt due to my meager performance compared to the rest of the class. I didn't mention this before, but each exam was 15%, and there was no final exam.

Regarding GeekOS, the TA's, especially Leo, really carried here. They were really helpful in getting some of the projects working, and I really wouldn't have passed the class without them. Though, I'd maybe argue they were a bit too necessary to get through the projects. It's very clear the project specs haven't been updated in years, and the project slides, especially for the later projects such as 4b and all of 5, don't seem at all sufficient in getting you through the projects. Of course, the projects should be challenging, but in my experience, there was a lot of frustration due to how much information the slides and specs omit. For example, in project 5, file systems, GFS3 is a completely proprietary file system, yet we're not really given a good specification of it. For example, we were only given one example GFS3 image whose structure is completely undocumented. In project 4b, demand paging (the hardest project imo, though I hated 5 more just by nature), the way in which we were basically required to do things isn't very easy to deduce from source code, and the slides honestly made it more confusing what we had to do. Don't get me wrong, these projects are pretty cool at the end of the day, and honestly it was very useful being forced to navigate and implement significant components into a Linux-like kernel. I just think the projects would be better if the provided resources were more helpful.

Finally, there's grading. The class is graded on a curve. This semester, seemingly a lot of insanely smart people took the class, which seemingly skewed the grade distribution like crazy. There was a review last semester of someone getting an 88 with Dr. Agrawala and ending with an A+. I know someone who got like an 89 this semester and ended with an A-. Take that for what you will.

Overall, I can't say I don't recommend taking this class at all, but I have some issues with it. Pete is teaching this class next spring, so it seems for a little bit, Dr. Agrawala and Pete are alternating teaching this class.

My review won't be as critical as the other one for this semester, but I share a lot of the sentiments about Pete and the class.  Pete himself admitted that his info about this topic in general is out of date one class, and his generally subpar lecturing style (very monotone) leads to a lot of confusion and difficulty understanding content.  We follow an online (free) textbook which goes into more detail, but a lot of the content on the exams is either difficult to find in the textbook or just something he put on a couple slides.  

The exams themselves aren't difficult given you scour the slides and your notes.  All the problems on the exam are either short form questions about certain topics or definitions, or questions you've seen before on homeworks.  

The projects are on the more difficult side compared to other 4XX classes, and set up similar to 417 where they're tangentially related to what we're currently learning about in class, but most of the work is figuring out how to implement the features within the existing GeekOS system.  I personally really enjoyed these projects, they were interesting and fun to work with.  The difference though between this class and 417 though, is that the project specs are rather useless.  They don't really help much with understanding what you're doing at all to be honest, and its hard to get a grasp of the scope of each project purely from the spec sheets.  It's not impossible, but there's a noticeable difference that leads to a worse experience.

If you are willing to put in the time investment, this class is a must-take, in my opinion.

Ashok's not good at lecturing. Exams are very difficult. I would prep around 30+ hours and take notes on every chapter of textbook and I got around 70, 90, 80 on M1, M2, Final respectively.

Projects are all doable, but take a long time... especially for debugging. The harder projects can take 20+ hours. Also, information about the project is scattered across a project spec, slides provided by the TA, and project overview discussions sections (which are not recorded). Make sure to go to discussion on days they introduce new projects. Make sure to start as early as possible so you can go to OH. The TAs carry the course.

Overall, your grade in this class mostly comes down to how much time you can spend on the class. I only took 3 classes this semester, and spent a lot of time for this class. The grade is split between (1) projects ~40, (2) two exams ~30, (3) final ~25, (4) participation ~5. No insight into how participation grade works, but projects can really help to boost your grade if you do them all on time :). I ended with an 89, and this was curved to an A+

CMSC412 with Ashok was difficult. I was forced to enter this class as there were no other  CS classless to take to fulfill my last reqs to graduate. I was very worried because this class was known to be difficult and if I didn't pass that would've caused all sorts of issues for me. For those students who are in Cs get degrees mode, you can get a C, you just will have to work very hard for it. The exams and projects are difficult. The projects are 40% of the class grade, if you go to office hours religiously the TAs can help you get unstuck fairly quickly. This way your project grades will be your saving grace even if you were bombing the exams like I was. There is a test bank that you can use to practice for them, they are found on neil's CS home page, google cmsc 412 home page and dig around you will find it. There were questions from tests from 1996 that were pasted onto our exams.

So, if you don't want to try very hard to pass, and you don't like OS, don't take this class. 
If you need to pass this class and you are a bit of a bum, then you need to do well in the projects, the office hours and recitations will help you and then you don't have to do incredible on the exams to pass. 

Those people who did not pass were the people who did poorly on the projects AND the tests. To pass this class you must choose between the projects or the exams to do poorly in. It is easer to do poorly on the exams, the projects despite their difficulty, if you use OFFICE HOURS ALOT, you will do well on them and do better than the rest of the class.

If you are wondering about a curve, or how the grading scheme is, Ashok seemed to be purposely unclear about curves or grading schemes.  But for my class, he must've had a generous curve based on me passing with my class grade of 68%  +/- the final ( one person passed with a 63% +/- the final) , we aren't quite sure how big the curve is because he never told anyone how they did on the final that was around 30% of the grade (hence the +/-).

The projects are extremely time-consuming and it can be hard to figure out what to do since the project descriptions are vague sometimes and specific instructions are scattered across the project slides, project specification document, and random Piazza FAQ sections posted by the TAs. Agrawala himself has almost nothing to do with the projects; the TAs are pretty much your only help.

The exams were difficult, but that's just the nature of CMSC412, so I can't blame Agrawala too much.

The syllabus didn't describe the percent that each assignment contributed towards our grade, so we were left guessing the weight of each one. We also didn't get our final back, so we have no idea how well we did, let alone what questions we got right or wrong.

Lectures are a complete snoozefest, but Agrawala can be quite funny sometimes.

The only saving grace is that there is probably a decent curve, so you'll probably pass.

This course was hard af, definitely a 4 credit. Peter helped make the exam aspect of this course manageable by closely relating his material to a digital textbook that was well written. His first exam was very difficult, but chilled out a bit afterward. The coding aspect was HARD. The projects required full attention, often spanning two weeks but sometimes overlapping with other projects. This course has a lecture and discussion, where discussion is fully project oriented. I was at every discussion and almost every office hour available in order to get a good grade on the project. Overall, I really enjoyed the course despite the rigor.
Honestly the exams are worse than the projects and the projects are terrible. Professor refuses to put in any effort whatsoever to make this class suck less.
terrible prof, terrible TAs. Refuse to make an elms page. website has wrong information. projects are very old, lecture has 0 to do with project.

I've had Shankar for CMSC 216 and CMSC 412. 

Although Shankar has a stutter if you focus during lectures, write down some notes, and ask him questions, he will clear up any confusions you have.  The difficulty of the exams he gives usually is written by whoever is proctoring the course. In CMSC 216, the exams given were written by Yoon so it was pretty hard. In CMSC 412, Shankar wrote his own exams, which were rather fair if you knew the material (much fairer than exams written by Yoon or Kruskal). 

The reason why I give Shankar 4 stars is literally because I think he did an ok job teaching 412. I think reviewing a professor's competence should account for the conditions of the course. The biggest change Shankar could've done is go over hints for the projects in the lecture, though this was mostly the job of the discussion section and the TAs. Other changes Shankar could've made were to make his slides less vague and provide more detailed practice exam solutions. 

412 is hard because doing the GeekOS projects take too long, leaving students without much time for other classes and to understand other aspects of Operating Systems not implemented in GeekOS. GeekOS is designed by a UMD graduate, Jeffrey Hollingsworth, Neil Spring, etc. If one accounts for the fact that this project was given to everyone who took CMSC 412, one would realize that this pain is not the fault of the Shankar but the curriculum of the course. Sure Shankar could've changed this curriculum but I don't think this would be too fair.

The review below isn't really telling of the in person situation at all. Sure, he may have been fine during Covid, but this class has been a complete nightmare in person. Like some of the other reviews below state, he was completely unresponsive to student questions and concerns, and as a result, the class suffered during his extremely convoluted projects and exams.

While I took this course during the Covid Times, this Professor was an absolute Godsend. His only requirement to be able to turn in projects late was that you talk to him in his office, which was always a pleasure. He understood the particular pressure that students in his course were under, and worked with everyone who asked on a modified submission schedule. I had never had that with a single CS professor before, and it felt as the Prof. Agrawala truly wanted students to learn. 

As far as actually teaching went, he was very knowledgeable about the material, and had first hand experience with the making of modern operating systems, which he shared with the class. His slides are yes from the text book, but they are always available on the class website, and line up exactly with the textbook, which he provided as a free PDF (I wish all teachers did this). As long as you read the book and practice any sort of problem that he does step-by-step with the class, as well as study the project slides, you have what you need to know for the exams. He doesn't list out topics for studying, but he also prefaces his course with advice such as, "get one last good nights rest tonight, that's it for the semester," and "everything you heard about this course is absolutely true." Regardless of if it is the case, it's imperative that you get stared on the projects early, and read the textbook. 

This is not an easy course, and this Professor understands that, but the difficulty in the course does not stem from administrative BS or weird rules. It's hard because Operating Systems are hard, and that's the point.
Worst class I've ever taken. Stay far away if you want to maintain your sanity.

This is one of those courses where the lecture has nothing to do with the project. The professor is decent lecturing about operating systems concepts, but you're stuck with the TAs to get you through the project which is probably the hardest project in your entire college career.

I would give ZERO stars if I would. This is both the hardest and worst course that I've ever had the displeasure of taking at UMD. I enrolled in this class because I thought that Operating Systems is a fundamental and useful skill to learn, even if difficult, but found out that the administration of this class makes this 10x more harder for literally no reason. There are so many things wrong with this course that I wouldn't recommend ANYONE taking it because it's not worth it. 

First of all, others seemed to like the professor's lecturing ability, but I did not. He goes on tangents all the time and is very unclear in his statements that it is impossible to focus. The slides are comprehensive, but are taken straight from the textbook so that isn't really a credit to the professor.

The projects and exams though, that is a different hell. Let's talk projects. Each one is incredibly difficult, and the instructions are HORRIBLE. There is really no valid reason why there should be a spec, slides, and FAQ for EVERY SINGLE PROJECT. The spec is awfully written and flat out wrong about things, the project slides are vague and also have incorrect information. The FAQs don't answer certain questions with any new information, and the fact that an FAQ is even needed for a project means that the instructions are poorly written. And to make things worse, even the spec, slides, and FAQ are sometimes not enough. 

On a related note, administration for this course was TRULY TERRIBLE. Questions on Piazza were just left unanswered even though there were many people with the same question; the TAs just didn't answer and weren't active. I'm pretty sure they were also left in the dark about logistics in the class, because it was near the end of the semester and we STILL did not have breakdowns of grading. That part of the course website was just never filled out. And one of our pop quizzes, which we only had 10 minutes to do and had a very poor average, was worth almost an entire project grade. That is completely ridiculous and shows how little the professor cares about administration for this class. For exams, we didn't get any review material, no study guide or previous exams, zip, zilch, nada. Just "look at the slides" which are hundreds if not thousands of slides so it's impossible to study everything on it. In addition, for our final, the professor was very unaccommodating to concerns over the Omicron variant, and refused to move the final online despite multiple CS classes shifting online, and almost the entire class requesting this change. No reasoning was given, of course. 

Lastly, our final exam, which is worth a quarter of our final grade, was put on the grade server, and we never even got it back to see what we got wrong, let alone a regrade request. It was simply put on Testudo. This fact may change since this review is posted, but nevertheless it is inexcusable to have these final grades submitted without students seeing the reason, especially when this resource is easily available via Gradescope. 

I get that Operating Systems is a hard concept, but like I said, the administration made this course needlessly more difficult. I am sure that most other people in the class agree with me regarding the majority of the points that I raised here, and there are probably more points that I didn't mention. These points are definitely fixable (having clear grading, clear project descriptions, enforcing Piazza answering, giving us study material) and should definitely be addressed the next time this course is taken. I find that unlikely to happen though, so I do not recommend this course to anyone until then. You're better off looking at the slides or textbook on your own.

Neil Spring is a pretty legit instructor. He clearly knows the material and the labs are actually quite helpful. The reason I'm giving him a 4/5 is because I strongly believe that the content of the class can really improve. We spent too much time learning synchronization primitives, and not a lot of time learning cool things like log-structured filesystems/networked filesystems, or the inner details of how a context switch actually takes place (something that I believe to be extremely important, yet this detail never really gets covered).

Lectures are pretty dry and difficult to follow. Exams are based mostly on lecture material, so looking at his online notes to prep is a must.

Projects are very time-consuming and specs are often frustrating as they do not accurately reflect what actually needs to be done in a clear way. By far the longest and most complicated programming assignments I've ever had in an academic environment; make sure to start early and ask lots of questions.

Overall, not a great experience. Maybe not quite as terrible as its reputation, but projects can get pretty ugly. Best bet is to take the class with people you know and discuss with them about the projects (at a high-level).

Professor: He does have a stutter, but if you pay attention you will have no trouble understanding him. This does however make his responses to questions slower than normal. He will also give tips on how to do well in his class and stuff like extra non graded assignments if you need more practice if you ask him. 

Coursework: Projects are very difficult. Start early (no really.) on all of the projects and be prepared to ask for help from the TA's. Exams are medium. He grades hard, but his cut offs are low. So even if you do bad on one test you can easily make it up. If you study you can do well on the tests. But studying can be a problem if you get behind on a project (projects are sometimes due 3 days before the exam date).   

Grades: He curves the tests and does something with the projects (I did badly on a lot of them yet still passed the class). He will not give you any extra credit or extra assignments if your doing badly. If you fail you fail.

Bottom Line? It will take a lot of work to do well or even pass this class. However you will learn a lot about OS's. Its also looks good on the resume and can give you a idea of how good of a programmer you are. Not recommended for a senior class unless you need 4 credits.

This is a horrible class. The projects are impossibly difficult and the professor is terrible lecturer. His stutter is distracting and notes are all over the place. Average for a midterm is around a 46/80. Exams are really difficut You will have to end up learning all of the material and then doing all of the projects yourself. Dont take this class with him if you dont have to.

I have a lot of respect for Dr. Shankar. He is extremely knowledgable on the subject matter. I did feel that too much of the course was spent on lectures about synchronization, but clearly this guy knows that stuff in and out. He does have a little bit of a speech impediment, but it didn't hinder his communication of the material to me in any way. We are all human right? Too many students used the excuse that they couldn't do a project because it wasn't heavily discussed in lecture, but not once have I had a CS course that went into detail about a project, not even 131! It may have been the fact that I was very well prepared for the course because of ENEE350. Shankar is very approachable, in his office or in class, much more so then most professors. He also spent the last class taking suggestions from students about how he can revise the course to better teach his students for the next time he is teaching it. How often do you see that? This guy actually wants his students to learn, and isn't out to make your life a living hell. His exams can be tedious, but they are definitely curved. He is a very fair grader, though you may find that your TAs are not so much. All in all the project is very time consuming, and is worth about 50% of your grade. The project though is not curved! I enjoyed this class a lot, and felt that this class really strengthened my understanding of a vast amount of topics.

Arbaugh was frequently absent from class and he had his TAs teach for him.  He took the projects from other universities, didn't do them himself, and rarely understood what was going on with them.  Given how frustrating this class could get, it's insulting that he doesn't seem to give a hoot about the class, when he's expecting us to spend 12 credits worth of effort on a 3 credit class.

Also, I'm sure some people knew that Arbaugh was planning on teaching 412 in Windows instead of a unix-based system, but they really, really need to put that in the course catalog or something.  Yet another thing Arbaugh could have done to make this class more reasonable.

In short, he sucks.  The only reason he didn't get a 1 is because he is actually quite knowledgeable.  He's not an idiot -- just a jerk and a flake.

Now, Neil is a great guy and a somewhat competent teacher. His teaching style takes getting used to; he basically walks into class everyday, opens up VI and just types notes, which you are expected to copy down and know. If you take notes on paper, learn to do it by computer, or you will get crazy pissed when he hops all over the place modifying what he wrote. My personal suggestion is Microsoft OneNote. Of course, he posts the notes file online, so you don't really need to take notes, but I would advise you do so, particularly if you're not that familiar with the subject.

He involves the class by basically asking us questions and writing the answers in his VI file. He writes it very colloquially which is nice, but sometimes he uses really obnoxiously large, outmoded words (draconian, pathological etc.).

The way the lectures go will be entirely up to you and your classmates. In my case, my classmates were total geniuses. We have 1 guy who got a diploma from MIT, half the robotics team, and a bunch of other people who basically know everything there is to know about linux.

These people will be the bane of your existence if you are not one of them. They will side track the class, ask really convoluted and (in my opinion) irrelevant questions, and basically confuse the HELL out of you.

It is basically your job to slow these people down and make sure they don't get too many opportunities to derail the class.

Neil also gives quizzes if someone's cell phone goes off in the class. So, study your notes every night basically. He also has a huge vocab sheet he posts at the beginning of the semester, with words that will be covered on his multiple choice exams.

Now some of you may have seen me say multiple choice, and grinned happily; set aside that notion, Neil's exams are pretty damn bad. His questions are more tricks than tests of knowledge, there are several that can be interpreted to mean different things, and it's really anyone's guess as to what they truly ask. Other questions can sometimes reword the answers in such a way that even if you know what the answer is, finding them among the choices is tricky.

The projects in this course are pure hell for the most part with 1 or 2 exceptions. This isn't really Neil's fault, he delegated it all to his TA, who mismanaged time a fair amount (routinely showed lecture slides for projects 3 weeks before they were ASSIGNED).

Overall, it's not easy to review this course, as I don't know if it's me, the TA, the professor, or the course itself that's the problem, but I do put in 40 ish hours a week for out of class work, and I have a C-.

Neil is a fair guy though, so I am not too worried about failing/passing.

If you want an A in this class, and haven't been weaned on linux, then you will need to start reading the book weeks before the semester begins. Make sure you have flashcards ready from a previous semester on DAY ONE of the class.

Look over previous semester's projects.

This class is more demanding than any other I have ever taken, and it's in no small part because of the disparity in intelligence of the individuals who take it.

It's going to be a tough, long, hard semester, but keep your head up, and prepare well, and you will get the grade you earn. If your time management sucks, however, prepare for a real shock to the system; this is one of the hardest courses offered at UMD, and you will find out why.

I would only recommend this class if you have a light semester or elite ball time management skills.
- Marsh uses a flipped classroom, where he demos random stuff during class and makes you watch videos on your own. The videos are far from enough to do the projects, but you can't just skip them and self study, because there's a Canvas quiz for each one.
- For the first 2 projects, there's a "follow up" where you live code in front of a TA. The coding tasks themselves aren't too bad, but the logistics are awful. There was a period where they ran out of appointments, and various announcements from Marsh and different TAs contradicted each other. It felt like they hardly communicated with each other and didn't coordinate plans at all.
- He uses "standards-based grading," where grades are based on checklists of assignment statuses. For example, you need x projects at 100%, x writeups at excellent, x writeups at sufficient, etc. This made things ambiguous when you didn't match checklists perfectly and were between letter grades.

FWIW, the class content is quite interesting imo and Marsh seems like a nice guy. He just has some really *creative* ideas on how to run a class.

The six straight 1/2 star reviews for Marsh 414 below me are nuts. First of all, if you just want an A (which is why I took Marsh), this is the best professor you could possibly have. I'm sorry but if you can't get an A in a class where there are no exams and your assignments are basically a bunch of completion grades + four projects that you have months to do, that's a skill issue. The projects aren't easy but they're all easier than some of the ones you do in 330, in my opinion, and that's a required course.

In summary - If you just want to coast, you can do that easily. And if you want to really learn the material, this class gives you the freedom and time to do so because you don't have to stress about exams.

Solely judging on how "easy" the class is, I would give it a 4 stars. The buffer overflows project was the only extremely difficult one, the other's just took some time, but nothing crazy.
In terms of how much I learned, I would give this class a 2 stars. I will say, I actually went to lecture 75% of the time so I probably got more out of the class than people who never went so that's on them. Marsh's teaching style was ... alright. I think a flipped classroom CAN work, but I don't think it was the best in this case, especially given the fact that there was SOOOO much content. (I also just find it really hard to focus when watching videos).
I don't agree with the reviews, below, it really was not that bad. Some of the quizzes were a little confusing, but you had unlimited attempts at them. His grading scale was also incredibly fair (he used a EMRN scale for writing instead of grading with numbers), and as long as you started the work before it was due, it was pretty manageable. I believe he's planning on removing the late deadlines, but this is probably a good thing. I know a lot of people let work pile up at the end of the semester and it hurt their grade.
The group project SUCKED, but mostly because I had a terrible group who waited until a week before it was due to even look at the project. The instructions were a little confusing but if you spoke with a TA or Marsh early it made a bit more sense. It wasn't necessarily hard, just a bit confusing on what we were supposed to protect against. 
There were also no exams which was a huge bonus in my opinion. 
I started the semester seriously freaked out about this class, but after I figured out the buffer overflows project, which admittedly took me forever, I found the rest to be pretty easy. Everyone says this but just start the projects early and speak to TAs or Marsh when you get stuck, it really helps.

Do not take this class. Flipped classroom whatever. when it comes to that part you should know yourself and your work habits. This is NOT the reason why I think this class was terrible though. Comparing my experiences to my peers, it's clear to see that which TA grades your projects/follow-ups/challenge problems decides too much of your grade in this course. This class is actually a sham and I genuinely think the CMNS department should review this course's scope and general practices. 

Marsh as a professor is a very good lecturer and I enjoyed his demos in class but again gave me nothing of value for any graded work in the class.

His lectures were pretty engaging and he's clearly interested in the content, but the disorganization of the class left a lot to be desired. Stuff doesn't get graded for a long time, like one project that took over a month to be graded. The final ended up online with little warning. His grading was also messed up for the final, which he had to correct (to his credit, he did fix it). The last project was a partner project and my partner wasn't added to the gitlab for an entire 2 weeks, despite the emails he ignored. I like his lectures, but I wouldn't take him again due to the lack of care he puts into the administration of the class.

Do not be fooled by his high rating: his rating is him as a person NOT as a college professor.

This is the worst organized class I have ever taken, with almost no communication at all from Dave about anything. It is less than 36 hours before our final as I'm writing, and he has not even told us the location of our final exam. Every other lecture involved him going on long tangents, either unprompted or from a malicious student question, about the research he does and how cool it is (with no connection to projects or exams).

He has not responded to one piazza post this semester, with one TA being in charge of that. However, to no fault of the TA, all of the actually important non-trivial questions are ignored/unanswered as they require an instructor to determine them. And of the questions that are answered, many are answered with "I will contact Dave and follow up", with no follow up, or "Have you tried contacting Dave?".

Speaking to the class as a whole: There is WAY too much content. It feels as though you scratch the surface level of 20 different concepts, and come out having really learned nothing.
Stressful difficult projects

Genuinely enjoyed the last project so ill bump him up a tad. Wish we were actually taught more relevant material but whatever. I dislike how his contract means everyone is at a C+ until the last day basically.

Genuinely the most useless class I have ever taken. We barely do any real security its all basic shit and nothing is taught in the class that actually helps you out, adding to the stress. The challenge problems and quizzes are tedious and annoying and also do not add anything to the class. I genuinely regret taking it with him but its a free grade I guess.

Yizheng was really nice when I talked to her and willing to explain things to help; frequent pauses were made at lecture to ask for questions, and there were always a few active students who were engaged and had interesting conversations. A LOT of the class did not attend regularly (probably in part because the exams mostly graded on slides) but there were good explanations of how the relevant architecture and network protocols led to vulns and i think everyone who actually went to class did well in it.

Abt the negative reviews below, I think the projects were relatively straightforward with a good autograder for the parts that were autogradeable. This class is terrible with this professor. The slides are useless, going to class is useless, the videos are useless. This was one of the most painful classes I've ever had to take. The class follows a flipped classroom, but the 50 videos that we have to watch before each class don't even help with the projects. I get that it's supposed to be challenging, but why aren't we taught on anything useful? We only do exercises in class that don't help with the projects. What is the point of paying so much money to study computer science when we keep on being told to figure it out. These are not projects that can just be figured out. The hate in here is not deserved, I do agree her class was more difficult than it should've been, but if you spoke with her she was especially kind and willing to help. It was clear to me she was definitely putting in the effort to be a better teacher.

Goat lecturer but just be aware his grading takes FOREVER.

projects and exams were really challenging and grades take a while to get back, but tas and class materials were pretty helpful with both of them

I also am not really interested in the class content, so that definitely didn't help. Also, one thing to note is that this class HEAVILY leans into computer security rather than network security.
