Good professor, generous grading, very nice person. 240 can get very jargony but she tries to tie it back to concrete examples which is nice.  She gives out practice exams a week before exams, and they're pretty similar. I would say office hours are the most helpful, she's very good at showing you the exact procedure for problems. She posts all her lecture notes. Quizzes during discussion are free points. Exams are not too bad. Matlabs are also not bad. Take her she'll give you a very fair class

Don’t let anyone tell you not to take her, those warnings usually come from people who aren’t willing to put in the work. Yes, the class is challenging, but that’s exactly what makes it so rewarding. She provides everything you need to succeed, from clear guidance to helpful resources, and pushes you to grow academically. By the end of the course, you’ll not only have a strong grasp of the material but also a better work ethic and confidence in your abilities. Truly a teacher who makes you better, highly recommend!
Lectures are kinda confusing to follow along with and so are her notes if you look back at them later. Tests are super easy, quizzes are super easy, and MATLAB is a free grade boost.

Professor Song is really nice. However, she doesn't teach the material very well, and it's hard to follow her notes. Yet, her quizzes are free points, and her tests are easy and similar to her practice tests. TA discussions are very helpful, most of the time I learned the material better from them. 3.5 stars.
She's gotten better honestly especially if you're taking Math240 I'd recommend her over Wong.

This professor has the most deceiving rating ever. He's a super-fast lecturer who doesn't post notes and record lectures, so if you have any conflicts on the day of a lecture, you're screwed. The way he teaches in class is in no way even close to what is on the exams, and his practice exams are deceivingly easy. His final is also 30% of the grade, so even if you have a perfect grade in the class, if you mess up in any way on the final, you won't pass the class. If you decide to take him for math240 be prepared to study an insane amount on your own time.

Professor Song is really nice, but she lowkey doesn't know how to teach. Granted, her lectures aren't that confusing and she posts all of her lecture notes on Canvas, but on some harder topics you might have to learn from the textbook since she doesn't explain them too well. She also sometimes gives gap notes that are really helpful for understanding the concepts that she isn't the best at teaching. Her exams are fair, and she gives 2 practice exams before each one that are super helpful. Some exam questions will be straight up the same as the practice exam questions. The MATLAB assignments are also pretty easy, but we've only done 2 as of two weeks before the final. The TAs are nice and the discussion sections are pretty helpful if you didn't understand what was taught during the lecture. There's a quiz almost once every week during discussion, but the prof basically tells you exactly what will be on the quiz and the TA will go over practice problems that are super similar to the quiz questions right before it. Attendance isn't mandatory but she doesn't record lectures.

He was honestly a nice professor, however, his lecturing style did not seem to work. He would write on the chalkboard, speed through examples and seemed to oversimplify or skip over steps to save time, which left a lot of people confused. Overall a nice guy, but if you need slower guidance or teaching for math I would not go for him.

My man Stefan is an absolute goat. He is an amazing prof that knows his stuff and he is also very approachable and helpful. His exams are fair, lectures are informative and organized (no bs), overall he is very chill, 10/10 absolutely recommend

Nice professor, she is relatively new to lecturing, so some of the lectures are a bit confusing in terms of formatting. I learned more from the TA office hours, discussions, and reading the textbook. Quizzes are super easy, she tells you exactly what is on it. Exams are of the same difficulty as the practice exams and do not contain trick questions. If you can self-study and ask questions, you'll do well.

Excellent professor. Very passionate about the course material and deeply cares about student success.  He remained my mentor afterwards, and guides me to consider going to grad school.  Really wonderful professor and mentor.

I took Stefan for MATH240 (Linear Algebra) my first semester as a student (and my first math class at UMD). He taught mostly straightforward. The textbook problems were helpful, and the TAs were willing to help. The exams and quizzes were very fair in my opinion. None of the questions were outside of what was taught in class or the textbook problems. Personality-wise, he always seemed very approachable after class to ask questions. Piazza was also helpful, and he would answer questions pretty quickly on there. I definitely recommend him for MATH240.
So goated. Makes discussions fun and teaches really well. Highly recommend him for any discussion he teaches

Dr. Khurana is an amazing professor. One of the hardest-working professors I've had. She holds 2-hour Zoom review sessions the day before each exam, going over problems on topics that the exam will cover. 

Lectures are also great. She makes complex topics very understandable based on what you already know. She also posts raw lecture notes on ELMS before each lecture, and posts the updated lecture notes shortly after lecture. This is really helpful for grasping the concepts before lecture and having a strong understanding after lecture.

Genuinely cares for students' learning. Highly recommend.

Really good teacher, goes over material really well and goes over examples in a way to help you think and understand the questions. Really knowledgeable and exams are extremely fair and doesn't throw any curveballs for the questions.

prof. khurana was an incredibly nice person in my (few) 1-1 interactions, but in general i came out of her class not feeling i gained much from her lectures (having most of it saved by my TA)

pros:
uploads lecture notes
lots of practice exams available 
solid weekly quizzes that tested my understanding of current topics, but w/o atrbitary/'gotcha' questions crafted solely to trip up students
textbook used (linear algebra and its applications by lay) was really well-written, and was a much better use of my time than attending lecture

cons:
lectures were formatted as follows: ~15 minutes of standing at the front of lecture hall, verbally reciting what had been covered previously (w/o any visual cues or worked examples to apply to - literally just her talking), followed by reading out of textbook/working textbook problem on her ipad w/o any real attempt to develop intuition (p much j "see how i did that? that's how you solve these types of problems"), which was projected onto a screen. would frequently ask vague/rhetorical questions, pausing lecture until somebody answered
very easy exams, to the point it felt that she was teaching to a 'lowest common demoninator' rather than giving any sort of challenge (ie the whiny kids in lecture asking "will this be on the exam???" "do we really need to know this?" "that's too hard!" ad nauseam) (looking at you cs majors)

the goat 🐐🐐🐐🐐

TL;DR - would genuinely recommend you go out of your way to get whatever TA discussion section he's running, was legit one of the best classes i've taken at UMD

- always showed up to class having looked over what he was going to be covering, w/ typed (!!!!!) tex notes of his own, +- any relevant programming examples in python or similar

- seemed to actually be excited (at least as excited as one can be teaching an intro lin alg course lol) about the cooler stuff we covered, bringing interesting/applicable examples of whatever topic (eg constant time fibonacci numbers w/ matrix diagonalization)

- really helped me gain intuition for what we were covering

- super nice chill dude, happy to answer questions (even goofy/obv ones)

i'm pretty sure she's leaving umd, as she just got her phd, but i wanted to write this review as an indirect thank you note. ran was my ta for linear algebra, and although the class was a bit confusing at first, ran's discussion sections were largely responsible for much of the concepts beginning to "click" for me. she would often give students extra time if they were struggling and would take time to explain a mistake if you got something wrong on a quiz. all in all, she was a great ta. her discussion section genuinely reshaped the way i studied for math (i actually started trying lol) and has motivated me to go past 200 level classes to take more advanced math. ran made getting an A in 240 extremely manageable, and i wish her the best in her endeavors post-umd.

no idea why his ratings are so low. sudheer was my ta for linear algebra and was genuinely so sweet and encouraging. i knew a lot of the questions i asked him during office hours were lowkey stupid, but he still answered them regardless--often giving follow-ups to ensure i actually understood the material. you can tell he truly cares about his students. he asks you what your name is and actually remembers it, which is extremely rare for any instructor to due in a class as large as 240. he also would check up on us, provide extra study material, and take hours out of his week to host exam review. not really much more you could ask from a ta. if you end up having sudheer as an instructor, know that you are in good hands.
He just didn't teach that well, I didn't find a reason to go to discussion other than for the quiz, and he just isn't engaging.
He's a pretty average prof. Gets the job done, teaches good enough, quizzes are fair. Midterms and the final aren't too bad.

Dr. Khurana made Linear Algebra one of the most rewarding math courses I’ve taken. She has a talent for breaking down complex topics into manageable pieces and building a strong foundation before moving on to harder material. Her teaching style is clear and structured, which helped me stay on track throughout the semester.
She’s also extremely supportive outside of class - her office hours were a great resource, and she was always willing to take extra time to make sure I understood the material. The quizzes and practice exams she provides really prepare you well for the tests. I left this class feeling confident in my understanding of the subject. I also appreciated the MATLAB projects, which the TA's provided a lot of guidance on.

Pretty good professor, Teaching style was originally in a follow-along lecture format but midway switched to handing out paper notes to go through as a class. TA was a big help but overall was able to understand concepts well just keep going to class and discussion

i literally didn't even do well and i'm giving her 5 stars. i had a rough semester personally and a lot going on outside of school, and i just didn't study for the first two exams and bombed them, and honestly most ppl probably would've dropped the class in my situation. i went to her office hours to talk to her and she was the sweetest most supportive professor i have ever talked to in my life. she was so so so encouraging and helped me calculate what i needed to pass the class, and provided me sm resources. then i studied for the third exam and did super well. her exams are so light literally just do her review problems in the packets she gives and youre set. even the final, do the review problems she gives you and you will be good.

yea, lecture is iffy and might not be helpful, but you can teach yourself the concepts using her notes and youtube, and get an A easily

He is a very nice and caring guy, but his lectures are hard to follow. He took directly from the textbook, but somehow his lectures lacked structure. I went to every lecture and consistently felt like it was a waste of my time. When I sat and listened, I gained a lot more than when I tried to write exactly what he was saying, because it was all over the place. 

With that being said, he is very helpful when you go to his office hours. When you take time out of your day to be there, he respects you and truly does want his students to succeed. So if you put in effort, he will give it right back.

The MATLAB assignments were super easy, especially if you worked in a group- I just recommend doing those way ahead of time so you aren't waiting until the last minute. I used Chat on all of them, and for the most part, it was accurate, still good to check it yourself, though, because you could lose a few points here or there (like I did). 

My one beef with Conway is that he doesn't give you practice exams that are his, and for the ones he does give you, he doesn't provide answer keys. So going into the first exam, I felt very unprepared because I didn't know his exam style, and that reflected in my grade, however, I was able to get it up. He asks a lot more theoretical questions than you would expect, so know the concepts and know them well, not just how to solve a problem. 

I liked him enough as a person, though, to take him again for 241, so take that as you will. My best advice is to go to his office hours and don't take shortcuts.
Good professor good grading mostly easy class

Conway is overall an awesome professor! Take him if you can!

I never went to his lectures because he provided dense lecture notes online, plus his lectures were recorded too (though the quality isn't that good but I check it out from time to time if I don't understand the notes).

You don't have homework assignments but rather 4 major MATLAB assignments that you can work with a group, and are quite do able in my opinion. There are quizzes almost every week on a set day during discussion (except exam weeks). I personally didn't do well on them because I was having a rough semester, but looking back on it, it's actually pretty easy if you spend time every week looking at the new material and doing some practice with it. I actually ended up doing better on exams, and yes like others said, Conway tends to be asking nitty gritty questions, but it's just like 1-2 questions, and I personally found his exams to be easy and do able.

Given his nitty gritty nature, take that as an advantage because I realized that I actually understand linear on a very deep level (and you definitely want this if linear is a core part of your major, I'm talking to you guys cs majors hahaha). And he preps for the final really well too given this nature. He's really kind and funny and approachable, he's just awesome!

Conway is overall a great professor! I didn't go to his lectures because it seemed pointless to me, especially when his lecture notes were dense and provided online (even the recordings too, though the quality isn't that good). I personally found his quizzes to be a bit challenging to me, but looking back at it, I realized they were actually darn easy, it's just that I was having a rough semester. Exams, unlike what others have said in the reviews, are actually pretty do able and easy (I always end up doing much better on the exams than on the quizzes). Yes he does test you on the nitty gritty concepts, but I actually kinda liked that because Conway will do an amazing job teaching you linear on a deeper level, and helping you get a deeper intuition behind it (and it's just like 1 or 2 questions at most that are like nitty gritty, most are just general linear exam questions to expect). You will definitely want this kind of professor if linear is like a core/key foundation behind your major (a la computer science). You also don't get any weekly homework assignments but rather 4 major MATLAB assignments that you can work with a group. They aren't that bad and it's kinda do able too.

He is very nice and approachable, and funny too. Definitely take 240 with him it's worth it.

She's really underrated. She explained concepts with sufficient depth and is always willing to answer students' questions. She gave us gap notes which I really appreciated because it allowed us to focus on lessons and not worry too much about copying down every little thing. The discussion sections are also well-designed, and the worksheets are very accurate to what quizzes/exams are like. For the three midterms, she gives two practice exams for each one, and sometimes also gives a review sheet. You can tell she really wants her students to do well in the class. She tells everyone the topics the weekly quizzes will cover which I've heard Conway does not do. Her MATLAB assignments are extremely light and she even drops your lowest one. She probably isn't as good as Archana, but she's really not a bad professor and I was able to get an A easily. Students may find some concepts difficult at first, but it is easy to succeed in this class. The one downside is that lectures aren't recorded so you do have to attend, and also that some topics were not clearly explained the first time but she goes over everything several times so it's not too bad.

intro:
overall i think i liked the class and coursework? if you want to know why 3 stars, see the cons section below
the class itself is not very hard and she makes the class pretty easy in multiple ways

pros:
- quizzes are given about weekly/biweekly depending on exams/break, and you can work in groups of 2-3 within your discussion section (so make sure you're in the same discussion as your friend if you care)

- she does a LOT of review sessions, for midterms and a couple for finals (which look generally useful if you're lost on a topic), mostly over zoom/recorded but sometimes in person; i never went to these but she gave useful info there
- she posts her edited/unedited notes on the ELMS files page so you can follow along and/or catch up, but very rarely the notes might not make any sense alone (without her explanations in lecture) if you don't already understand the foundation/previous content that its building on

- midterms/finals were, for me, easier than the practice versions or the review session problems 
- couple of points of extra credit on exams
- 2 quizzes dropped?
- she seems very kind and helpful
- discussions are mainly extra practice problems for content you're on, and i didn't attend after 2/3 of semesters when things got busy and I still did well overall (besides required for quizzes)

neutral:

- the way that the notes are written during lecture can sometimes be messy. there's a general format of definition/theorem -> examples but this can change from time to time
- 4 matlab projects, i found the content/questions asked here somewhat more confusing than in-class, and sometimes its a little unclear of what the question exactly is asking for/how you can get to the answer, but overall not a bad part of the course
- she has a decently heavy accent which if that's hard for you to listen to/understand, it could be a possible issue
-- additionally, shes not fluent in english like a native speaker, which is fine, but you just have to be more careful when listening to make sure you understood correctly
- sometimes makes a mistake during lecture which slows down the class which is fine overall

cons:
- here's my MAIN issue with the class: going to lecture was such a terrible experience (for me)
- besides the accent (for me personally), she had very odd/fluctuating pacing throughout each lecture; she would either be really slow with question/problem making it boring, or be really fast with a question and you can't write any notes down
- on top of pacing, sometimes she'll be late and then hold the lecture for like 2-3 minutes after class and only slightly mention "this will be really important: ..." after doing miscellaneous work the entire lecture
- she repeats herself like, a lot. like 3-5+ times at certain points in lectures. then she might also move on quickly and you won't know if shes still on the same example #1 or suddenly on example #10
- she always expects class engagement in the lecture (or even in review sessions). she'll either like have the answer up on the screen and then ask us for the answer (literally waiting for someone to say something), or she'll just repeat a question like 4 times asking what the answer is (even if its painfully obvious/basic arithmetic)
- she switches between an ipad screen/her paper notes at times, slowing down  class but also why can't we just stick to the screen format which is easier to read/follow along
- explanations for concepts are IFFY at BEST, and generally just not helpful at all. she'll switch through a various bunch of concepts quickly and sometimes you'll fall behind on what's going on in class (or she'll move backwards in content while you're still writing down an example) --> THIS was honestly one of my bigger issues; her explanations are just not good
-- additionally, I just didn't find her explanations useful for new concepts and I was often rather confused after a lecture on what she meant. (but it does seem like she knows what shes talking about)
- she has a lot of expectations of what terms you understand/know and will quickly mention some new word/vocab in class but not actually explain what it means so its like a double layer of confusion
- overall, i just had such an entirely bad experience with attending her lectures i pretty much dreaded the days I this class's lecture
- lectures themselves are not recorded if you care


conclusion/tldr:
- class was on the easier side and shes very helpful, kind, and provides many resources to succeed but the lectures were approaching unbearable (for me).

Archana is a very kind professor and takes a genuine interest in ensuring that students who put in effort get a good grade. She holds review sessions for the three midterms and multiple for the final regardless of how many show up. These helped me in understanding concepts the most out of all resources. Quizzes are during discussion and you can take them in collaboration (two get dropped). If you understand what is going on in the quizzes you most likely are up to speed with the class. Overall, she is lenient, genuine, and nice, and if you are ever struggling in the course go to her office hours and she will help you without hesitation as long as you are genuine. Just make sure to stay attentive in lecture or you may find yourself lost after a few lectures.

Archana is probably one of the nicest professors I have had so far at UMD. She genuinely cares about the success of her students and always answers questions students have either after class or over email and provides very comprehensive reviews before the exams. However, that being said, I felt like sometimes her explanations were extremely lacking. I often would have to read the textbook, or watch videos to understand the topics discussed, as her lectures often confused me, even though the material of this class is not that difficult. The class was fast paced to start but quickly became slow to the point where it was a struggle to pay attention. The few difficult topics in this course were poorly explained and were one of the few things that actually felt rushed. She often repeats herself multiple times within the span of a few minutes, which somehow makes things more confusing. She also makes quite a few mistakes in lecture which can get annoying at times and sometimes will just randomly pause for several minutes trying to figure out what is going on and what she is trying to say, which is extremely frustrating. After lecture I often questioned why I bothered showing up, as I think reading the textbook could have been a better use of my time since I would read it anyways to understand what was discussed in class.

I think she is one of the better math professors in the department and is wildly over hated for no real reason. Her lectures can be boring at times, but she has a great way of explaining things to people who have never looked at any linear algebra before this course. She gives out guided note sheets, but she also posts her notes in case you miss a class. There was 3 MatLab projects and 1 that she gave us an automatic 100 on. There are weekly quizzes that require minimal studying, because the TA normally goes over the topic right before the quiz. The exams are incredibly fair and with just a few hours (like 2-3) of studying I was able to get As on all. Overall, I really recommend taking this course with her and she is the reason I have decided to take 401 in the fall.

A bit of context, this is now a post-semester review being written roughly a week after final grades locked in. I already left a mid-semester review, where I gave Zheng only 4 stars to balance out the immediate 1-star review that someone left only 3 weeks into the semester. Now giving my afterthoughts:

As the more recent reviews have already said, Zheng definitely improved over the semester, so I won’t restate everything they covered. I mainly want to give some context for why the early reviews were so harsh.

After Midterm 1 (with an average of ~76), the GroupMe turned into an echo chamber where a vocal group of students circulated the same complaints for weeks. One of those students made a Google doc listing the issues with Zheng, and people in the chat were explicitly encouraging others to leave 1-star PlanetTerp reviews based on these complaints. That doc later got cleaned up into a printed letter addressed directly to Zheng, asking whether he could provide extra credit, more practice problems, drop the lowest midterms, etc. This letter was then left at the back of class for students to sign if they wanted to.

To be fair, I’m not sure Zheng would have become as lenient as he did if that letter hadn’t happened, so some of that pushback was probably warranted, even if it shouldn’t take something like that for changes to happen in a class.

Personally, I thought the Midterm 1 practice was definitely enough. I skipped a few problems that clearly weren’t exam-relevant, but most of them lined up with lecture examples or homework. Some questions were basically the same concept with different numbers. I get why people were frustrated, but a lot of the “nothing like the practice” claims were overstated. For Midterm 2 and the final, the practice was even closer to the exams; arguably too close in some cases.

Zheng's sections were originally meant to be taught by Anurag Dey, who is known for being an "easy A" according to his PlanetTerp reviews for STAT401. We got switched to Zheng about a month before the fall semester started (i.e., during summer break), so it's possible that the same people were expecting that kind of class and were frustrated when the difficulty didn't match those expectations.

I agree with another recent review that 3.5/5 is probably a more accurate rating, but I’m giving a 4 just to round up and reflect the improvement and to help improve the average. Zheng has shown he has the capacity to improve, communicates fairly well given the language barrier, and is certainly not the "worst" choice for STAT400 as other reviewers had initially put it.

Given that we are only 3 weeks into Zheng's first semester of teaching, I'm only giving 4 stars just to balance out the review below. This is by no means a complete review, though it doesn't immediately justify giving someone a 1-star for that reason.

The lectures are loosely based on a drafted version of lecture notes from Jonathan Fernandes and Mestiyage Gunatilleka, both of whom are historically high-regarded professors for STAT400. There are gaps of explanation during the lecture; some parts feel glossed over, likely unintentional due to the nature of reading off the draft notes. There have also been some observable moments of language barrier, such as reading "Independent Trails" instead of "Independent Trials", or some handwriting issues mid-lecture that students occasionally have to raise their hand to question what was written, or correct the professor in writing P(B|A) instead of P(A|B).

According to Zheng, if he had to put a number on the difficulty of the coursework, he mentioned the following towards the end of the first lecture:
"Homeworks are... like an 8/10"
"Exams are, 5/10"
"The quizzes, these are like 2/10"
"The homeworks are by far harder than anything you will see on the exam"

As of now, we've only had one homework (no homework was assigned during the first 2 weeks). There were four problems, each one reflecting what we learned in class: basic combinatorics, binomial trials, geometric probability, and the inclusion-exclusion principle. They do not expect you to know the answer just from the lectures alone - it is explicitly encouraged to use outside material (internet included) when completing it.

The first midterm isn't till October, the second one isn't till November, and the cumulative final is in December. I cannot speak for how the exams go until then. Whether you choose to go to the lectures is up to your learning style: Are you actually incentivized to study outside of class? Or would you do better with a primer in-person?

Until then, take the preceding reviews with a grain of salt.

As others have said, Archana is a very very kind person (regardless of what you think about her teaching). She tries to get to know every student in class, especially those who go to lecture and remain active in office hours. 

She has lectures which are pretty well organized. She first explains some of the theoretical concepts, and then does some textbook problems on the board or on chalk. She has this raw and updated lecture note system which you'll learn more about if you take her course that is pretty helpful for some (for me, I never had the time to look at the notes before most lectures in the first place and didn't have an iPad so it wasn't particularly remarkable). If you don't use an IPad to take notes, definitely go to her office prior to class to get print-outs of the notes so you can have some of the notes already there that way you won't have to write problems or long theorems that she won't spend more than 2-3 minutes on by hand. 

Regarding her teaching, I will say there are times where it feels like she doesn't know the topic in depth (especially in stats). For example, she struggled to explain Bessel's correction for sample standard deviation the first time it was taught in class. This doesn't interfere to teach what she thinks is necessary for the course and exams, but it gives off a murky vibe if you're interested in going a bit more beyond surface depth of what's taught in the course and if that interest comes out in the form of asking more complicated questions in class, especially for some of the things in the hypothesis-test section of the course.

There are typically quizzes and worksheets in the class that are done on ELMS/Canvas every lecture or so with some being graded and others being for practice. Archana tends to be lenient about this but it can be a pain in the ass to do sometimes, especially because (this is a me thing specifically), I would get lazy and just use GPT or some other thing to do them instead of doing them by hand. There are also projects in the course, but I also used GPT on those. While they give real world applications to what is being taught in the class, they're really just extra work that doesn't correlate with the exams and some of the material we need to know so a lot of people would do the least amount of work possible for them.

Now, it is also worth mentioning, I do fundamentally dislike the curriculum for the course. It is pretty much ALL performing hypothesis tests, which are rarely performed anymore by hand (yay for computers). So, you end up getting an extremely in-depth introduction to how to use various hypothesis tests to understand and analyze different data trends, but a lot of this information is useless in modern day statistics simply because machines can do a lot of it for us. While she strived to give a big picture analysis of how to use the techniques (something that would last a lot longer than the individual mathematical techniques we learned to perform each of the tests in the class), I will say that the impression I got was that the class was simply focussed on performing many of these tests by hand and not taking a set of data and deciding what to do with it in order to determine the trends.

I would have preferred if we maybe cut the time we spent on discussing how to compute various sources of error, and strict computations of the different hypothesis tests (during the course, you will study one-sample and two-sample z-tests for means and proportion, t-tests for means, confidence intervals, power and error in various tests, anova tests, chi-squared error of tests, error of linear regression with normal residuals, and using the central limit theorem to discuss normal random variables or random variables that converge to the normal distribution), and instead discussed how to decide which statistical tests to use for a given set of data, and how to run such experiments: for example, "how would you go about setting a statistical procedure to get data for determining whether this new feature increases user engagement on a site?". Learning a bit more about sampling (just an introduction), deciding how to filter data, and then picking the hypothesis test and describing the procedure, would have probably been more helpful for your average person who might go into a stats/data-science field in their life at this point of time with technology.

This all being said, this is a very very common thing among all STAT401 courses and I suspect this is more of a departmental curriculum thing than it is Archana's fault. Thus, I will not take this out on her rating. BUT, if you're a student, be prepared that the class is heavily computation-focussed, and you will have to learn how to apply some of the techniques to broad data on your own, or in other CMSC/STAT classless such as STAT440, CMSC320, CMSC471, etc

The last thing that is worth mentioning about Archana is that, especially in my semester, she sometimes did call people out in class. If you weren't paying attention, she would probably ask "why weren't you paying attention" or something in a kind way (not aggressive at all and you can definitely say "I don't know"). During exams, she would sometimes say how specific individuals did -- let's suppose there is a student named "Arnav" in the class, she might say something like "Arnav, you didn't get that topic on the exam, why did you not get it? Did you not prepare and do the practice problems? Were you not slow enough on the exam?"... things like that can sometimes be huge turn-offs for those who really respect their privacy on exams. She is NEVER doing this out of malice however, and you will notice that even if she does it, she's doing it in a respectful and encouraging way trying to uplift and encourage students to put more time and effort in the course. Just something worth noting for shy students.

Overall, Archana is a very kind person, and you should definitely get to know her regardless of your interest, performance, and participation in the class by going to her office hours and simply showing up at every lecture and striving to sit in the front and remain somewhat engaged. Her accent is absolutely fine and easy to understand, and you're going to learn a lot in the course.

Most of the content you will learn are asynchronous which makes lectures either redundant or near useless 9 times out of 10. But you can't just not show up to lecture, there are graded in class group activities which are also useless and I'm 99% sure you could pass comfortably with an A even if you didn't get those points. There are times where an actual new or interesting concept will be introduced in lecture but more often than not you will walk away wondering what you actually learned in that 50 minute period. 

As for coursework the bulk of the grade comes from 4 exams, one of which is dropped. Most of them are relatively easy if you have any programming experience at all but there's a few questions that are about very specific techniques in python. The 3 homeworks throughout the semester are sort of the projects you would expect of a programming course which aside from the final project are the most time consuming. But even then if you have any programming experience at all you could finish one in 1 or 2 hours and you have unlimited attempts so you can just keep debugging and resubmitting until you check all the boxes which is nice. Considering this is the main programming course of the info sci major, I can't say this course had the rigor I expected. Maybe that sounds great to some of you but if you're expecting a programming course that has any difficulty then this is not it. Even the final project felt like a softball and the hardest part was getting your group members to commit and push to github. 

Most of the other assignments are just you explaining certain concepts in your own words and then provide working examples yourself which I find would be unhelpful to anyone learning python for the first time. 

And everyone else talking about the grading is not making it up. I kid you not, I waited until a few days before final grades were due and I got everything graded all at once in the span of an hour. So don't expect to get any grades back throughout the semester or know what your grade is at all. 

Overall the course structure felt really unorganized and most of the assignments weren't all that helpful aside from the homework's and group project. I'd recommend him if you have a decent understanding of python so you can just coast through the class without too much concern because if you are trying to learn python from this course, you're in for a rough time.

I enjoyed this course and the assignments we had. I would say that it's important to supplement course material with your own understanding via YouTube, online resources, etc... as lecture felt more like covering some examples and were more like "here's a concept, now let's try it out" but I think that is realistic for a programming course. I did have prior Python experience, and I was a bit lazy with submitting assignments, but I thought the assignments were fairly straightforward and reasonable and still managed to get a "reasonable" grade. I think if you're the type of person who's willing to do a little bit more research/follow-up besides ONLY what is learned in class, you'll find this course to be fairly straightforward on 95%+ of the assignments.

We'll get it out of the way: he's a great guy, tries to remember everyone's name, and definitely wants people to learn. He also had a monologue at the end of class about using coding to do good in the world which I thought was very sweet. 

The class utilizes a flipped classroom format: you have to watch a series of videos about the subject of the week, do a small assignment due before class, then a small group assignment on Monday, Wednesday goes over content and Friday is supposed to introduce most stuff for the week. I don't dislike this format inherently, but a lot of the lectures are just repetitions of the content. Sometimes it dipped into genuinely neat material, but most of the time I walked away from class thinking "why did I come here?" My only answer was for the participation credits, which is never great.

Exams feel a bit at cheap at times, but with four non-cumulative exams they aren't the worst thing in the world. Homeworks hold your hand a bit too much, the group project has some very strange requirements about using very specific techniques. Our group assignment was to make a game, but the scope of what a game was defined as was extremely nebulous. Besides the group project, I didn't really feel like any assignment took up an unfair amount of time, especially given that this is the MAIN programming course for InfoSci. It could've afforded to go a little further and more in-depth, but the flipped classroom format gives you the skills to look things up.

Also, the comments about grades taking forever to come in is true. It's not fun not knowing where your standing is in the class, and I was almost certain of where I was. Group project felt really rushed, we straight up had multiple assignments get auto-100%'d because of how far behind on grading he was. Very excited about the material, and I still would recommend him, but he could stand to use time better in lecture/on the schedule in general, and generally have a more organized class.

I think everyone says it pretty well for Bills as a teacher but I'll my say: Aric Bills is a really great person, he's really supportive, understanding, and fun to talk to and has a lot of humorous/fun interactions with the actual class. He is very active on support people outside of the class in my personal experience and I think everyone does appreciate his kindness and his patience.

But in teaching, I think it could be improved. His current method of teaching his students is through videos that students must watch in their own time, alongside an small assignment due essentially every monday 9 am. These videos can be a bit long overall with some taking 1-2.5 hours in watch time total. Grades weren't uploaded to canvas and so you'd have to input them by hand to canvas from gradescope if you wanted to know your grade but even then his grades on gradescope were very delayed (after spring break for some reason?). There was a point where it gotten 2 months behind and it was a bit frustrating seeing that.

You don't need to go to the lectures or discussions, as the discussions were mock office hours & I think this whole semester he only hosted a virtual session 3 times? Lol. The one time he did have a live session, I waited about 30 minutes and he never showed up, so I don't recommend trying to go to them and just going to office hours instead for help (assuming half the class isn't also there). Here's a list of everything for my non-paragraph readers like me:

Pros:
- Asynchronous, do not need to go to the lecture or discussions unless you wanna
- Easy assignments, usually 1-2 a week, can do most in a few hours or less
- Forces you to be better at python if 126 didn't help you (like me)
- Do not need teacher-student interactions, goes at your own pace (pro for me as I did not need to ask for help, I only needed to discuss grades, but that did not end up happening as I am still waiting for a reply)
- Self-paced, I once did 3 weeks of content in 1 week because he opens everything at the start of the semester

Cons: 
- Very hard to contact instructional team for it being an asynchronous class, you would hope that this would be a main priority
- A lot of the assignments have not been updated since 2021 and have just plain wrong instructions that no longer work with the current version of python OR outside links have not been updated and new ones are not provided. In these cases, you just need to find it and figure it out yourself. 
- Even though I got better at python, I still felt I learnt nothing from this class since the slides and readings do not correlate much with the assignments
- If you are a visual learner (i.e. like seeing code examples to base your own off of) this is not the class for you. Try Bills instead (if you can put up with exams and overhype that is)
- The TAs make or break the class unfortunately since the Professor doesn't do much for the class. You just have to pray that a strict TA isn't grading the heavier assignments
- Hard to talk to other students about the class since there is no lecture, so you're basically on your own (this can be a pro too depending on what you like/need)

Then, there’s an in-class group coding exercise due Wednesday morning, meaning you’ll probably spend Tuesday working on it. You might have a homework assignment due on Friday, but if you’re lucky, there may be nothing. Additionally, there are 4 exams throughout the semester and they are always on Wednesdays every 2-3 weeks.

On exam weeks, you still have to complete the plethora of weekly assignments. While he sometimes eases up by making the exercises easier during these weeks, there’s still a lot to do. The excessive amount of group work required, often needing to be done outside of class, makes it hard to coordinate with everyone and takes up all your personal time. The final project is also a group project, and while it may seem easy it can be incredibly unorganized at times.

I am never at peace since the to-do list is never done. While I didn’t expect to breeze through this class, this is a little too much to bear. The professor is passionate about the topic, but in my opinion, it’s just not worth the stress.

- For lecture vids, have your screen split half vid, half jupyter lab to take notes (highly recommend taking notes in jupyter lab as the graded practices are jupyter notebooks)
- In class don't just sit and watch him go over concepts, take notes during this time. - Do all work ahead of time, especially homeworks!! Office hours are your best friend.
- Try to scout out people you want to work on the final project ahead of time, (would recommend sitting closer to the front of the class and finding people who are always present in class and work hard)
